articles.title: Zelensky says Ukraine ready for ‘de-escalatory steps’
articles.body:
Zelensky says Ukraine ready for ‘de-escalatory steps’
KYIV – Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said on Sept 14 that Ukraine was ready to de-escalate the war with Russia if its rival did the same, after US President Donald Trump announced that the foes had agreed to end strikes on energy targets.
With international oil prices climbing again, Trump had at the weekend berated Ukraine’s attacks on Russian refineries, blaming them for causing a shortage in diesel fuel.
In one of his surprise social media posts, the US leader announced on Sept 14 that “Ukraine has agreed not to hit Russian energy targets. Russia has agreed to do, likewise!”
Russia made no immediate comment. But in his daily address, Zelensky highlighted “a strong proposal from the United States regarding a mutual halt to strikes on critical infrastructure”.
He added: “If this can become the first de-escalatory step – stopping Russian strikes on our critical infrastructure, and ours in response – then Ukraine is ready to support de-escalation.”
Zelensky said “we see that the Russians are feeling pressure because of our precise responses against Russia’s war economy”.
He noted that “so far no one has seen any genuine desire from Russia to move towards ending the war”.
“But if our American partners succeed in securing a real readiness from Russia to stop this war of destroying lives, and to do so sincerely and for the long term, Ukraine will make its own de-escalatory steps.”
Rail strikes get worse
Trump has insisted that the Russia-Ukraine war, and not the conflict with Iran, was driving up fuel costs for Americans who vote in crucial midterm elections in November.
A previous push by Trump for a ceasefire has been sidelined by the US-Israeli conflict against Iran, now in its seventh month. US envoys went to Moscow and Kyiv earlier in September without announcing a breakthrough.
While Ukraine has hit refineries deep inside Russia, Zelensky has stepped up calls for allies to provide more anti-missile defences as Russia intensifies its attacks.
Russian strikes on Ukraine’s rail network are worsening each week, the chief executive of the state Ukrainian Railways operator told AFP on Sept 14, after a strike hit a train frequently used by diplomats near the Polish border at the weekend.
“It’s growing exponentially. Each month, each week is generally worse than the previous one,” said Oleksandr Pertsovsky.
NATO member Poland said on Sept 13 that Russia hit a train about 2km from the Polish-Ukraine border, just days after Kyiv officials said road crossing checkpoints on the border with Moldova had been targeted.
Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk said on Sept 13 that Warsaw had obtained information that Moscow might be planning attacks on border crossings.
EU delays sanctions deadline
But European Union countries on Sept 14 delayed a deadline for prolonging sanctions on Russia after France pushed for billionaire Alisher Usmanov to be removed from a blacklist, diplomats said.
An EU list of almost 3,000 individuals and entities – which needs to be extended every six months – was set to expire by Sept 16.
However, ambassadors from the 27 EU member states pushed back the deadline one week after the late efforts from Paris to remove 73-year-old Uzbek-Russian metals tycoon Usmanov drew opposition, the diplomats said.
Usmanov, a former major shareholder in Arsenal football club, was placed on the EU sanctions list in 2022 over what Brussels said were his close ties to the Kremlin.
The French move surprised some EU states.
“Renewal of the listings is essential to continue undermining Russia’s war machine, and keeping the pressure on those individuals and entities supporting, enabling and benefiting from it,” a spokesman for Ireland, which currently holds the EU presidency, said.
The Financial Times reported, quoting people familiar with the issue, that France was making the push as part of a prisoner release deal involving French citizens held in Azerbaijan. AFP

articles.title: Russian regions report Ukrainian strikes as Rostov governor cites 'massive' missile attack
articles.body:
Elena Teslova
15 September 2026•Update: 15 September 2026
Ukrainian missile and drone strikes hit several Russian regions early Tuesday, with Kyiv confirming attacks on an oil refinery and a drone production plant as Russian authorities reported damage to residential, industrial and commercial sites.
Rostov Governor Yury Slyusar said the region was subjected to a “massive missile attack,” with damage reported in the city of Taganrog.
An educational institution, commercial building, gas pipeline, agricultural warehouses, grocery store and Ozon warehouse were damaged, Slyusar said on Telegram. Taganrog Mayor Svetlana Kambaeva said five apartment buildings were also damaged, but reported no casualties.
Reports also indicated damage near the Taganrog Aviation Scientific and Technical Complex, although the extent and circumstances were not immediately confirmed by regional authorities.
Ukraine's General Staff said its forces struck the Atlant Aero plant in Taganrog, which it said manufactures drones.
In the Samara region, more than 40 drones were shot down overnight, Governor Vyacheslav Fedorishchev said. An industrial facility and several residential buildings were damaged, but no deaths were reported, he added.
Ukraine's General Staff said its forces struck the Syzran oil refinery, reporting a fire and damage to a crude oil distillation unit and storage tanks.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy also confirmed strikes on the Syzran refinery and a drone production facility in Taganrog. He said Ukrainian forces had also struck a drone preparation and launch site in the Oryol region and targets in the Black Sea.
In the Voronezh region, Governor Alexander Gusev said the attack damaged windows at a municipal building as well as the roofs and facades of four private houses. No casualties were reported, he said.
Meanwhile, the Russian Defense Ministry said its forces carried out group strikes with attack drones on logistics centers and ports in Ukraine, as well as vessels it said were used by the Ukrainian armed forces.
In the Odesa region, the ministry said a logistics center used to store and distribute military cargo arriving in Ukraine from abroad was hit in the settlement of Velyka Balka.
At the port of Chornomorsk, a dry cargo vessel and a ferry that the ministry said had delivered cargo intended for the Ukrainian armed forces were also hit, it added.
Russian forces also continued strikes on railway infrastructure in western Ukraine used to transport military cargo from European countries, the ministry said.

articles.title: Gas Stations Hit, Explosions Rock Kyiv as Russia Launches 200-Drone Attack
articles.body:
Russian forces attacked Kyiv with drones early Tuesday, Sept. 15, killing one person and injuring at least seven others, while UAV strikes and falling debris damaged buildings and gas stations across the capital, according to Ukrainian officials.
The Kyiv City Military Administration (KMVA) announced an air raid alert at 5:25 a.m.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
At the same time, the Ukrainian Air Force tracked jet-powered drones entering the Kyiv region and heading toward the capital before subsequently appearing over the city itself.
Explosions were heard in Kyiv at approximately 5:34 a.m. and again at 5:42 a.m.
Kyiv Mayor Vitali Klitschko later reported on Telegram that a Russian drone had struck a gas station in the city’s Darnytskyi district, injuring one person.
“Medics hospitalized one wounded person. The man is in critical condition,” he wrote.
He also said that, according to preliminary information, a warehouse facility in the Obolonskyi district had been hit.
A drone threat was announced in Kyiv again at 7:49 a.m. At around 8 a.m., Kyiv Post reporters heard a very loud explosion.
Klitschko subsequently confirmed that a UAV had apparently struck a non-residential area in the Solomianskyi district.
“Emergency services are en route to the scene,” he added.
In an 8:51 a.m. report, Klitschko said heavy smoke was reported in the Holosiivskyi district following a drone strike on a gas station.
NATO Jets Shoot Down Drone Over Lithuania
“Two people have already been wounded in the morning attack on the capital. Medics have hospitalized both of the wounded,” the mayor said.
Klitschko later clarified that the number of casualties had risen to four. All four are being treated in city hospitals, with two in critical condition.
The State Emergency Service (DSNS) later reported that eight people in Kyiv had been injured by Russian strikes since the start of the day.
“Solomianskyi district: a non-residential building was hit; no fire broke out. Six people were injured,” the report said.
Rescuers also confirmed that a gas station in the Darnytskyi district had been hit, injuring one person. The resulting fire was minor and was extinguished with fire extinguishers.
“Holosiivskyi district: a strike occurred at a gas station. One person was injured. The fire has been extinguished. Obolonskyi district: a non-residential building caught fire. Firefighters have brought the blaze under control,” the DSNS added.
In a 10:35 a.m. report, Klitschko announced that one of the people injured in the morning attack on the capital had died in hospital.
“The man had been hospitalized in critical condition,” he added.
187 drones downed or suppressed
According to the Ukrainian Air Force, Russia launched 200 strike UAVs against Ukraine starting at 6 p.m. on Sept. 14. The attack included Shahed-type drones, including jet-powered variants, as well as Gerbera and “Parodiya” (Parody) decoy drones.
The attack was repelled by Ukrainian aviation, anti-aircraft missile troops, electronic warfare and unmanned systems units, and mobile fire groups.
“According to preliminary data, as of 8:00 a.m., air defense forces had shot down or suppressed 187 enemy UAVs,” the Air Force said.
Russian drones were recorded striking seven locations, while debris from downed targets fell at three other sites.
This story will be updated as new details become available.

articles.title: Danish parties support government response after Russian frigate fires flares near helicopter
articles.body:
Danish political parties broadly support the government’s response after a Russian frigate fired two flares toward a military helicopter Monday, according to Denmark’s Armed Forces.
Defense Minister Jeppe Bruus of the Social Democrats briefed party representatives Tuesday. The Foreign Ministry has summoned Russia’s ambassador to Denmark, Vladimir Barbin, to discuss the incident.
“It is completely the right thing to do,” said Inger Støjberg, leader of the Denmark Democrats, a Danish right-wing party.
The Armed Forces reported the incident in a statement at 11:02 p.m. Monday. It said an Air Force Fennec helicopter was taking routine photographs of the Russian frigate in international waters off Gedser.
The frigate fired two flares, which are normally used as attention signals at sea. One passed close to the helicopter.
“It is obviously an escalation from the Russian side,” said Thomas Danielsen, defense spokesperson for Venstre, Denmark’s Liberal Party.
Alex Ahrendtsen, defense spokesperson for the Danish People’s Party, urged calm.
“Of course, we should not go to war with the Russians because of some signal lights that have been sent up,” he said.
Bruus said both the frigate and helicopter had a right to operate in international waters and called the helicopter’s work normal.
Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen of the Social Democrats described the incident as serious but unsurprising.
She said it was part of a pattern involving “an increasingly aggressive and assertive Russia” that is testing NATO and conducting hybrid warfare against Europe.
“Russia wants to intimidate and sow discord. Our response is to stand closer together and strengthen the defence of Denmark and Europe,” Frederiksen said.
Train services between Fredericia, Odense and Copenhagen returned to their normal schedule at 10 a.m. Tuesday after damaged overhead wires near Sorø were repaired.
Trains between Copenhagen Airport and Slagelse also resumed normal operations, Banedanmark, which manages Denmark’s rail infrastructure, and passenger rail operator DSB said on X.
Banedanmark warned that some delays could occur while services restart. It advised passengers to check Rejseplanen, Denmark’s public journey-planning service, before traveling.
The damage had caused cancellations and delays since noon Monday. Repair work covered the section between Ringsted and Slagelse.
Banedanmark described the repairs as “extensive” and “very complex.” A support cable had fallen, and the equipment holding it had also been damaged.
“These are just some of the damages we see on our traction power system,” Banedanmark maintenance director Nicolai Sigsgaard said Monday.
Banedanmark received the first report of the problem at 12:45 p.m. Monday. Train traffic was then stopped completely while workers identified the cause.
DSB and Banedanmark said passengers delayed by more than 30 minutes could use DSB’s travel time guarantee.
DSB paid 67 million DKK in passenger compensation during the first six months of 2026, more than twice as much as during the same period in 2025.
A delay of at least 30 minutes provides a new ticket for the same route or a refund of 50 percent of the ticket price. Passengers delayed by an hour can receive 75 percent and claim up to 75 DKK for food and drinks.
Delays exceeding 90 minutes qualify for a full ticket refund.
A 31-year-old man held in custody over an assault that led to a Swedish man’s death at a Copenhagen World Cup event will appear in court on October 7.
The hearing will begin at 1 p.m. at Copenhagen City Court, the Copenhagen Police prosecution service said Tuesday. A formal indictment has not yet been filed.
The man is suspected of punching the 32-year-old Swede hard in the jaw or neck. The case falls under Section 244 of Denmark’s Penal Code, which covers less serious violence.
The incident happened June 30 during a public screening at Islands Brygge of the World Cup match between Norway and Ivory Coast.
The Swedish man fell after being struck, hit his head and later died from his injuries. He worked for the Swedish police but attended the event as a private citizen.
The 31-year-old suspect, a Danish citizen who came to Denmark from Congo as an infant, has been held in custody since July 3.
Two other men, ages 24 and 29, are also suspected of violence connected to the event.
The 24-year-old Danish citizen is suspected of stomping on the Swedish man while he was lying down and hitting another Swedish citizen.
The 29-year-old, a Somali citizen, is suspected of kicking the second Swedish man. Police have notified him of the charge by telephone and through his defense lawyer because they have not located him.
Police have said the three cases will be handled separately because there is no evidence that the men acted together. Court dates for the other two men have not been announced.

She said it was part of a pattern involving “an increasingly aggressive and assertive Russia” that is testing NATO and conducting hybrid warfare against Europe.

A citizen proposal seeking tighter controls on untreated wastewater discharges has received the 50,000 signatures required for consideration by the Folketing, Denmark’s parliament.
The proposal, titled “Discharge of untreated wastewater into streams, watercourses, fjords and the sea,” was published September 3 and reached the threshold 10 days later, the Folketing said Tuesday.
It will now be submitted to parliament as a motion for a resolution.
The proposal contains four measures. The first would require flow meters at every wastewater overflow in Denmark. Data from the meters would be published on a digital platform, allowing the public to see how much untreated wastewater is discharged.
The second measure would require an authorized analysis company to take regular water samples and test them against 14 European Union requirements for chemical measurements.
The proposal would also introduce a fee for discharging waste substances that are diverted around treatment plants without being treated. Its final measure would require every overflow structure to have a valid permit.
The proposal received attention after Amanda Heitmann, a member of parliament for Venstre, Denmark’s Liberal Party, signed it.
Venstre’s environmental spokesperson, Marie Bjerre, reprimanded Heitmann for supporting the citizen proposal.
“As a political party elected to the Folketing, it is not our job to sign citizen proposals, but to take a position on the content,” Bjerre told Politiken, a Danish newspaper.
Heitmann was also one of five Venstre lawmakers who recently went against the party line and voted against the fertilizer act in parliament.
Russian frigate fires flares near Danish military helicopter in international waters
A Russian frigate fired two flares toward a Danish military helicopter in international waters off Gedser on Monday, Denmark’s Armed Forces said.
The Fennec helicopter was taking routine photographs of the ship when the flares were fired. One passed close to the aircraft, according to a military statement.
Flares are pyrotechnic devices normally used as attention signals at sea. No personnel were injured, and the helicopter was not damaged.
Danish Defense Minister Jeppe Bruus of the Social Democrats called the incident serious and described Russia’s actions as “very unprofessional seamanship.”
“It is serious. It is an expression of the boundaries having been moved regarding the willingness to take risks from the Russian side,” Bruus said.
Foreign Minister Lars Løkke Rasmussen will summon the Russian ambassador to discuss the incident, though the date of the meeting has not been announced. Bruus said he did not expect further action beyond that meeting.
The defense minister said the incident would not change Denmark’s monitoring operations.
“We view it seriously, but it is not the case that we will change our behavior, understood in the sense that we have a completely legitimate task in monitoring what is going on,” Bruus said.
Inger Støjberg, leader of the Denmark Democrats, a Danish right-wing party, said the incident showed that Russian provocations had reached Denmark.
She called for NATO unity and continued support for Ukraine in its war against Russia.
“It is therefore crucial that NATO stands united, and that we continue to support Ukraine,” Støjberg said. She added that she expected a briefing from Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen.
Danish electricity prices head for most expensive month in years as gas costs rise
September could become the most expensive month for Danish electricity customers in several years, energy company Norlys said.
Halfway through the month, the average electricity price was 1.11 DKK per kilowatt-hour in western Denmark and 1.12 DKK in eastern Denmark.
It is the first time since December 2022 that the monthly average has exceeded 1 DKK per kilowatt-hour, according to Norlys.
“We are halfway through September, so a lot can still change, but with the rising gas prices, we unfortunately have to expect that it will be an expensive month,” said Ellen Trolle, director of Norlys’ energy business.
Electricity prices were set to rise above 7 DKK per kilowatt-hour Monday evening, their highest level in almost two years.
Norlys said the increase was caused by higher gas prices and limited electricity production from wind and solar power. Natural gas plants often supply electricity when the weather does not provide enough wind and sunlight, making power prices more sensitive to gas costs.
Kristian Rune Poulsen, an analyst at Danish energy organization Green Power Denmark, also pointed to gas prices.
“The conflict in the Strait of Hormuz, which doesn’t really want to come to an end, means that a great deal of the liquefied natural gas that we have become so dependent on cannot get out onto the world market,” he said.
Poulsen said prices would continue to fluctuate but were unlikely to fall soon while the conflict continued.
“We expect that the elevated price level will persist throughout the winter, as it looks right now,” he said.
Nearly 12 percent of Danish ninth graders fail to pass Danish or mathematics exams
More than one in 10 Danish ninth-grade students failed to earn a passing grade in Danish or mathematics in this summer’s final exams, new government figures show.
The Ministry of Education said 11.8 percent of students did not receive at least 2, the minimum passing grade, in one or both subjects during the 2025-2026 school year.
“It is too high a proportion. Because it means that they initially will not have the opportunity to move on to youth education programs,” Andreas Rasch-Christensen, a school researcher at VIA University College, a Danish higher education institution, told DR, Denmark’s public broadcaster.
DR reported a failure rate of 10.5 percent, while the ministry listed 11.8 percent. The difference is that the ministry included students whose schools did not register that they sat the exam. DR excluded those students.
The result marks a small decline from the previous school year, when 9.9 percent failed to pass Danish or mathematics. The rate was 10.1 percent in 2023-2024 and 6.9 percent in 2018-2019.
The average final exam grade was 7.3, in line with the previous four years, DR reported.
The figures follow the release of a PISA study showing that Danish students’ performance had declined in reading, mathematics and science.
The government said similar declines were occurring across much of Western Europe. Danish politicians have pointed to mobile phones as a possible cause, saying quick stimulation from phones may make it harder for students to concentrate.
The government wants to introduce a complete ban on mobile phones in schools.
Lower food VAT would cost Danish businesses about 725 million DKK a year to administer
Lowering Denmark’s value-added tax on food would cost businesses about 725 million DKK annually in added administration, according to a parliamentary response.
Tax Minister Jakob Engel-Schmidt of the Moderates said Monday that the government wants to lower the general VAT rate on food and remove it from fruit and vegetables as soon as possible. The changes will not take effect this year.
“It is of great importance to the government to make it cheaper for Danes to fill their shopping baskets,” Engel-Schmidt said at a consultation.
The estimate is uncertain because the government has not decided how the new VAT system would work. Shops and other businesses would have to cover the administrative costs.
Dansk Industri, the Confederation of Danish Industry and Denmark’s main business and employers’ association, said the actual cost would be higher.
“When the VAT rules for food become more complicated, it affects the VAT accounting in virtually all active businesses,” tax policy chief Jacob Bræstrup said.
Bræstrup said the change would affect more than wholesalers, supermarkets and restaurants. He said total administrative costs would be “significantly higher” than the estimated 725 million DKK.
The broader proposal would cost the state 17.4 billion DKK a year, according to the Ministry of Taxation and Growth.
Leading economists have criticized the plan as an expensive and inefficient way to help people. They warn that businesses might not pass the full tax reduction on through lower prices. Some savings could instead pay for administration or increase company earnings.
The government plans to present several possible models in the second half of 2026.
Extensive damage to the overhead wire system near Sorø is expected to disrupt train services between Ringsted and Slagelse until 10 a.m. Tuesday, according to Banedanmark, which manages work on Denmark’s rail network.
One track has reopened after DSB, the Danish passenger train operator, stopped services on the section around midday Monday. Trains are now running on a reduced timetable, with longer travel times and some cancellations.
Tony Bispeskov, DSB’s head of information, said priority would be given to international, InterCityLyn and InterCity trains.
Banedanmark said it received a report of problems with the overhead wire system between Sorø and Slagelse at 12:45 p.m. Monday. Train services were stopped completely while the cause was identified.
“There we can see that we have extensive damage to one of our tracks. At the moment, this means that we only have one passable track to operate on, and that we are running with a reduced timetable,” Banedanmark said.
Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen of the Social Democrats said Monday that she is “quite optimistic” Denmark, Greenland and the USA can reach an agreement on security and defense in Greenland.
Frederiksen spoke at a news conference in Finland, where she attended a European summit focused on security in the Arctic.
“We have agreed to start a high-level working group on closer cooperation on security and defense, also in Greenland,” Frederiksen said.
“As long as the working group between Greenland, Denmark, and the USA continues its work, it is too early to draw a conclusion. But I am quite optimistic that we will succeed in finding a way,” she said.
Frederiksen visited Greenland last week with European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen.
Denmark is among 10 NATO countries conducting a joint military exercise in Greenland. The exercise is intended to show that Denmark and NATO are protecting Greenland and the Arctic.
US President Donald Trump has criticized Denmark for not doing enough to protect Greenland from threats posed by Russia and China.
During the first weeks of September, 400 soldiers from 10 NATO countries are operating on land, at sea and in the air near Narsarsuaq and Kangerlussuaq. They are training to operate in Arctic conditions as part of NATO’s Arctic Sentry surveillance and deterrence mission.
“If one is to be able to operate in the Arctic, one has to train up here,” Søren Andersen, head of Denmark’s Arctic Command, told the Danish news agency Ritzau last week.
Andersen said the temporary Arctic Shield exercise is part of a long-term strategy for Greenland and the Arctic.
“For us, it is about helping to transform NATO’s northern flank into a hard target. Meaning all the way from Alaska across Canada, Greenland, and to the northern part of Norway,” he said.
Denmark and Greenland are also discussing whether to give the USA greater access to Greenland. The New York Times reported in the spring, based on American sources, that the USA wants three bases in Greenland as part of a possible agreement. Narsarsuaq and Kangerlussuaq were reportedly among the possible locations.
Danish Defense Minister Jeppe Bruus of the Social Democrats declined to discuss the working group’s talks during a visit to Narsarsuaq last week.
“I cannot comment on that. What goes on in that working group, goes on in that working group,” Bruus told Ritzau.
Bruus said the government wants to extend the operating period of Narsarsuaq Airport by one year if it receives support from the Folketing, Denmark’s parliament.
“Initially, it is a one-year extension. That gives us the opportunity to extend the playing board,” Bruus said.
Chief of Defense Michael Hyldgaard said Narsarsuaq would be an obvious possible location for an American base because of its position in southern Greenland and its access to transatlantic routes, the Denmark Strait and the GIUK gap.
The GIUK gap is the sea area between Greenland, Iceland and the United Kingdom. It is an important military passage where NATO can monitor and block Russian submarines moving toward the Atlantic.
The USA previously operated a military base in Narsarsuaq from July 1941 to November 1958.
CPH Half will expand to 45,000 runners for its race on September 19, 2027, because of high demand, organizer Sparta Atletik og Løb, a Danish athletics and running organization, said in a news release.
Around 35,000 people are taking part in this year’s half marathon, up from about 32,000 in 2025.
Tickets for the 2027 race will be sold through a lottery instead of on a first-come, first-served basis.
Registration for the lottery opens September 16 and remains open for two weeks. People can register alone or in groups of up to three. Each group will either be selected together or not selected at all.
Selected runners will have 48 hours to buy a ticket. The price is DKK 795 plus a small administration fee.
“When demand is so high, access to the bib numbers must also function in a way where everyone has a fair and equal chance of getting a bib number,” Dorte Vibjerg, CEO of Sparta Atletik og Løb, said in the release.
The organizers also used a lottery to sell tickets for this year’s CPH Half, which is part of the World Athletics Road Running Championships. Similar systems are used for major marathons in Berlin and London.
This year’s race starts Sunday. Elite international runners will begin first, followed by the other participants.
Danish police brought 79 new charges linked to possible crime-for-hire cases from January through the end of July, the Ministry of Justice said Monday.
In total, police brought 316 charges from April 2024 through the end of July this year that may involve crime-for-hire, a practice also known as “Violence as a Service.”
The figures come from NSK, a Danish police unit that handles serious and organized crime. In January, authorities had recorded 237 charges, according to figures released by the ministry in February.
The government disclosed the latest figures as it sent a bill proposing stricter penalties and other measures against gangs and crime-for-hire for consultation. That process allows judges, lawyers, police and other groups to submit concerns or objections before the proposal moves forward.
The bill would increase penalties for crime-for-hire and treat criminal families in the same way as gangs.
“We will not tolerate children and young people being recruited into a life of crime, and residential areas being marked by fear, control, and parallel power structures,” Justice Minister Nicolai Wammen of the Social Democrats said in a statement.
The proposal would also add a provision to the penal code intended to make it easier to convict people who provide minor services to gang leaders.
Other measures include allowing background checks for dockworkers and increasing the penalty for violating a stay ban. Police have recorded a large increase in such violations.
A stay ban can be imposed on a person who has committed a crime connected to a gang. It prevents that person from entering a specific area, such as part of a town or municipality, for a set period.
Violating a stay ban currently carries a fine of 10,000 DKK. Under the proposed law, a violation would result in 30 days in prison.
Power and diesel prices heading for nearly two-year high

According to Troels Skipper, commercial director at OK, the high electricity price is due to a combination of rising gas prices and a lack of wind and solar energy.
“Right now, we are in the unfortunate situation where the high gas price pushes the electricity price up along with it. And unfortunately, we do not get enough electricity production from wind turbines and solar cells to push the price the other way,” he said.
The last time the hourly price was at around seven DKK per kilowatt-hour was in December 2024.
Also, Diesel prices in Denmark rose to a record high on Monday, reaching 19.19 kroner per litre after an increase of 20 øre, according to FDM, the Danish motorists’ association. Petrol prices also increased by 40 øre per litre. FDM consumer economist Ilyas Dogru said the increases followed the weekend’s escalation in the war involving the United States, Iran and Israel.
Denmark is set for a week of changing autumn weather, with periods of rain, sunshine and mild temperatures, according to the Danish Meteorological Institute, DMI.
Monday began cool, particularly in central Jutland, where temperatures fell to between 6 and 8 degrees.
“The temperature is down to 6-8 degrees, so if you are going out cycling, you can clearly feel that autumn has arrived,” DMI duty meteorologist Jesper Eriksen told Ritzau.
The rest of Monday is expected to remain dry, with a mix of sunshine and clouds. Temperatures will reach between 15 and 18 degrees, with light to moderate winds from the west.
### Tuesday to be warmest day
Tuesday is expected to be the warmest day of the week.
Winds will turn to the south, bringing slightly warmer air over Denmark and pushing temperatures to between 17 and 21 degrees.
There will be periods of sunshine, although some rain is possible, particularly in Jutland.
More rain is expected to reach Jutland later Tuesday afternoon before moving east during the evening and overnight.
Wednesday will bring some sunshine but also showers.
Temperatures are expected to fall back to between 15 and 18 degrees, while winds will turn west again.
Thursday and Friday are expected to bring periods of rain and showers, with temperatures remaining between 15 and 18 degrees.
Winds from the west and southwest are also expected to strengthen gradually toward the end of the week.
Eriksen said the week would not be particularly cold despite the unsettled weather.
“In the week as a whole, you will not need the really warm clothes, but in periods you will need rainwear and rubber boots,” he said.
It remains unclear whether September will bring another spell of warmer weather later in the month.
“We will have to see what happens, whether the last spasms with some warmth arrive. It is not decided yet,” Eriksen said.
More than half of the Danish schools that were selected for the latest Pisa survey declined to participate. In total, 398 schools were drawn for the survey. Of those, 215 chose not to participate, writes Kristeligt Dagblad.
When a selected school chooses to decline, a reserve school could step in. In advance, two reserve schools had been designated for each of the drawn schools.
Therefore, a total of 283 schools ended up participating in the survey. However, this is significantly fewer than in 2022, when 347 schools participated.
According to Kristeligt Dagblad, the number also remains below the OECD’s “technical minimum requirement”.
According to Monika Klingsbjerg-Besrechel, chief consultant at Statistics Denmark, which was responsible for the practical part of the survey, the many declines have not affected the quality of the survey.
“Fortunately, we reached a higher response rate, but despite that, we were unfortunately still below the minimum requirement from the OECD. If we had not had the reserve schools, we really would have been in serious trouble,” she says to Kristeligt Dagblad.
She points out that it was subsequently investigated whether the many declines had affected the result.
Silkeborg debuts as first host city for Royal Run 2027
Danmarks Idrætsforbund (DIF) has announced Silkeborg as the first of five host cities for the 2027 edition of the Royal Run, making it the first time the Central Jutland city is on the bill for the event.
“I am wildly happy about the news that we will be a host city for Royal Run in 2027, and I am looking forward very much to welcoming a public celebration in running shoes right in the middle of Silkeborg,” said the city’s mayor, Helle Gade.
Thus, the run moves to the city that also brands itself under the name ‘Denmark’s Outdoor Capital’, something the mayor looks forward to showcasing.
“Here in Søhøjlandet we have a unique setting for both participants and spectators with hilly landscapes, great viewpoints over the Silkeborg lakes, and an exciting city center where urban life and nature merge. I look forward to showcasing that.”
In 2026, the host cities were Randers, Ringkøbing, Middelfart, Helsingør, and Copenhagen/Frederiksberg. This year, Denmark can expect new cities other than Silkeborg to join the Royal Run host club, with a new host city scheduled to be announced every day this week.
The Royal Run offers three distances to run, including 1.6 kilometers (also known as one mile), five kilometers, and ten kilometers.
The event first took place in 2018, when the then Crown Prince turned 50 years old. Since then, it has been held every year on Whit Monday.
Last year, a record 112,450 runners participated.

articles.title: US confirms it has weapons in space
articles.body:
US confirms it has weapons in space
Published September 15, 2026last updated September 15, 2026
The United States has weapons deployed in spatial orbit, the US Space Force said, confirming the existence of such capabilities for the first time.
"The US has on-orbit space control weapons capable of defending the Joint Force against hostile adversary action," a US Space Force spokesperson said in a press release. The statement did not provide specifics on the weapons in question.
"Space control encapsulates the mission areas required to contest and control the space domain — employing kinetic and non-kinetic means to affect adversary capabilities," it said, adding that "these capabilities can be employed for offensive and defensive purposes."
US Air Force Secretary Troy Meink also confirmed the existence of US weapons in space, while speaking at the Air, Space and Cyber Conference on Monday.
The Space Force, the US military's arm dedicated to space, justified the weapons deployment by citing its two biggest geopolitical rivals — Russia and China. It said both countries pose a threat to American interests in space.
China "develops and operates space and counterspace capabilities as part of a military modernization strategy," while Russia "views space as a warfighting domain and believes space supremacy will be a decisive factor in future conflicts," the statement read.
What have China and Russia said?
In response, China urged Washington to "stop preparing for war" in outer space.
"We urge the US side to stop expanding its military capabilities and preparing for war in outer space," Foreign Ministry spokesman Guo Jiakun said, warning against an "arms race" in space.
Russia on Tuesday also called for space to be kept free of weapons.
"We believe that space must be free of any weapon," Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov told reporters in Moscow, adding: "We are counting on broad international consolidation to continue working toward the complete demilitarization of space."
The final frontier
The militarization of space is an issue as old as the race to space itself.
In 1967, the world's biggest superpowers and other nations signed the Outer Space Treaty addressing the single biggest concern — the deployment of nuclear weapons in space.
Since then, Russia, the US, India and China have been exploring ways to fight in space outside of that treaty. That includes targeting each other's satellites critical for military communication, navigation and surveillance.
Edited by: Natalie Muller

articles.title: Polish government funds TV campaign on emergency preparedness
articles.body:
Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work!
Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support.
Poland’s interior ministry has launched a TV campaign, including spots on public broadcaster TVP’s flagship morning show, aimed at educating the public about how to respond to emergency situations such as natural disasters and security threats.
The initiative comes as Poland has faced growing threats from Russia, including acts of sabotage and the entry of missiles and drones into Polish airspace. Prime Minister Donald Tusk warned this week that there may be an “escalation” of such actions in the coming weeks and months.
📺 Dzisiejsza wizyta w programie „Pytanie na Śniadanie” odbyła się w ramach naszej nowej kampanii „ Minuta dla twojego bezpieczeństwa”!
Rozmawialiśmy o sprawach fundamentalnych – o bezpieczeństwie. Mogliście sprawdzić, czy wiecie, co oznaczają sygnały alarmowe oraz krok po kroku… pic.twitter.com/ARta1Pqmlz
— MSWiA 🇵🇱 (@MSWiA_GOV_PL) September 8, 2026
The new campaign will include weekend segments on the TVP1 channel and a series of pieces aired during TVP2’s breakfast show, Pytanie na śniadanie, which had an average audience of 322,000 in August, according to Nielsen Media data.
The weekend programmes will introduce topics such as floods, fires, extreme weather, power outages, chemical contamination, evacuation, cybersecurity, disinformation and first aid. Specialists will then discuss the subjects in greater detail during the morning segments.
The ministry says the content is based on its official security handbook, which it sent to all 17 million Polish households earlier this year, and is intended to help people prepare for emergencies before they occur.
“We only find out whether we’re prepared for difficult situations when they actually arise,” said Mateusz Jarecki, who is presenting the segments. “That’s why, in collaboration with specialists, we’ve produced a series of short, easy-to-follow videos that will help you prepare for various life scenarios.”
The government is sending copies of a booklet advising how to prepare for and act in emergencies to all 17 million households in Poland.
The guide includes information on what to do in the event of military attacks, terrorist threats and natural disasters https://t.co/xIaRQ2ie5N
— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) January 12, 2026
According to Presserwis, a newsletter by media industry magazine Press, the ministry will spend 5.4 million zloty (€1.3 million) on broadcasting the campaign during Pytanie na śniadanie.
The agreement with the public broadcaster, signed on 4 September, includes 16 short segments and seven commentary pieces, according to Presserwis.
Pytanie na śniadanie’s website so far shows two segments with material from the series. One explains what to do when an evacuation order is issued, while the other covers what should be included in an emergency kit.
The campaign comes following recent criticism from the opposition over how the government communicates with citizens during emergencies.
Amid Russian mass attacks on western Ukraine this week, including strikes on a train and a truck near the Polish border, residents of eastern Poland received mobile phone alerts from the Government Security Centre (RCB) warning of air strikes and urging them to seek shelter.
However, Beata Mazurek, a senior figure from the opposition Law and Justice (PiS) party, criticised the messages for “spreading panic without providing instructions” on where people should shelter.
“Where are we supposed to go? That seems to be the most basic piece of information. The threat is real, but the instructions are incomplete,” she wrote on X.
Pani poseł @beatamk zablokowała komentarze, więc odpowiadamy tutaj.
Jeśli nie wie Pani, co zrobić, gdy wyją syreny – zapraszamy na nasze szkolenia. Uczymy tam https://t.co/yklFDaNeI3., jak zachować się w sytuacji zagrożenia i przygotować plecak ewakuacyjny. To wiedza, która… pic.twitter.com/V6je9VOUda
— Karolina Gałecka (@K_Galecka) September 13, 2026
In response, interior ministry spokeswoman Karolina Gałecka invited Mazurek to attend training sessions provided by the ministry.
“There, we teach, amongst other things, how to behave in an emergency and how to pack an evacuation rucksack. This is knowledge that comes in handy precisely in such situations,” wrote Gałecka.
Last December, the interior ministry launched a mobile application and website that helps people to find their nearest shelter.
In July this year, opposition figures also criticised the government when a Russian missile entered Polish airspace and landed in a field. They claimed that local residents were not provided with clear warnings and information about the threat and how to respond.
The object that crashed in the Lublin region on Thursday was a Russian Kh-101 cruise missile carrying a "significant amount" of explosive material.
The missile was "potentially very dangerous,” Poland's defence ministry confirmedhttps://t.co/NoqZwIcaWp
— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) July 31, 2026
After this week’s Russian attacks on western Ukraine, Tusk warned that “we can expect the coming weeks and months will be a period of very intensified Russian actions”, and that “we cannot rule out that this escalation will also affect our territory”.
Earlier this month, after an arson attack on a drone plant in Poland likely carried out by agents working on behalf of Russia, interior minister Marcin Kierwiński warned that “society must be prepared for the possibility of an increase in Russian acts of sabotage”.
A report published earlier this year by the International Centre for Counter-Terrorism found that Poland is the “primary focus” of Russia’s growing campaign of sabotage in Europe.
A drone has struck a passenger train travelling between Kyiv and Warsaw, around 2 km from the Polish border, amid the latest mass Russian attacks on Ukraine.
Separately, a truck around 800 metres from a border crossing with Poland was also hit last night https://t.co/ZbfE2iDLOk

articles.title: 'Reckless' — Russian frigate fires flares at Danish military helicopter near Denmark
articles.body:
For illustrative purposes only. A Fennec military helicopter flies during a military drill on March 16, 2016, at the military air base of Solenzara on the French Mediterranean island of Corsica. (Pascal Pochard-Casabianca/AFP via Getty Images)
A Russian frigate fired two emergency flares toward a Danish military Fennec helicopter in international waters near Denmark, with one passing "within a short distance" of the aircraft, the Danish Armed Forces said Sept. 15.
The helicopter was conducting "routine" monitoring of the Russian warship near Gedser, Denmark's southernmost town, when the flares were launched, according to the Danish military.
The incident has prompted Denmark to summon Russian Ambassador Vladimir Barbin, as Danish officials condemned what they described as an unacceptable act toward the country's military.
Danish Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen called the incident "reckless action from Russia."
"Russian actions are meant to intimidate and divide. They will not succeed," she said.
Foreign Minister Lars Lokke Rasmussen also described the incident as "completely unacceptable."
The incident comes as Denmark, a NATO member, faces growing tensions with Russia while also dealing with pressure from U.S. President Donald Trump over Greenland.
In October 2025, Danish defense intelligence said Russian warships had aimed weapons at its naval vessels and disrupted the country's navigation systems.
Yevgeniya Doluda is an intern at the Kyiv Independent. She is currently in her final year at City St George's, University of London, studying journalism, politics, and history. Yevgeniya previously worked and volunteered with non-profit organizations in Europe, and had her work published in RTL.
The General Staff said nearly 300,000 losses were roughly equivalent to the personnel strength of 150 motorized rifle regiments, based on an estimated 2,000 troops per regiment.
U.S. Special Envoy John Coale said the U.S. has urged banks to unfreeze Belarusian assets and is working on a mechanism to make their release possible.
The General Staff said a direct hit and fire were recorded at the Syzran refinery, part of Russia's state-owned oil giant Rosneft. The AVT-6 primary oil refining unit and the facility's tank farm were hit, according to the statement.
"If the Americans hadn't backed away from the Anchorage agreements... we would have been living without war for a year now," Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov said.
Alongside the attack near the Polish border, Russian forces launched 200 Shahed-type attack drones, including jet-powered versions, on Sept. 15, the Air Force said.
Ukraine's parliament dismissed Prosecutor General Ruslan Kravchenko on Sept. 15, a week after he resigned and a day after he announced that he had approved charges against the head of the country's anti-corruption bureau.
The incident has prompted Denmark to summon Russian Ambassador Vladimir Barbin, as Danish officials condemned what they described as an unacceptable act toward the country's military.
"With Russia intensifying its aggression against Ukraine, such readiness is vital for our region. Together with our NATO Allies, Lithuania will defend its airspace," Lithuanian President Gitanas Nauseda said.
The EU now has until Sept. 22 to renew its sanctions on 2,600 Russian entities and individuals. Attempts to reach an extension agreement have been stalled by calls to remove Russian billionaires from the list.
The couple described Russian oligarch Umar Kremlev as a "dear friend" who generously funded a three-day party for the Trumps in the Bahamas with no political motive whatsoever.

articles.title: Wilsbach Shares Airmen’s Stories of Epic Fury, Says 10 Got Battlefield Promotions for DUDE 44 Rescue
articles.body:
NATIONAL HARBOR, Md.—Ten Airmen received battlefield promotions for their roles in the daring rescue of DUDE 44, the crew of an F-15E Strike Eagle that was shot down over Iran this spring, Air Force Chief of Staff Ken. S. Wilsbach announced Sept. 14.
Wilsbach revealed the promotions—a rarity in the Air Force—and more details about Airmen’s actions during Operation Epic Fury in a keynote address at AFA’s Air, Space & Cyber conference.
Over the course of Epic Fury, which lasted from Feb. 28 until a shaky ceasefire in early April, the U.S. struck more than 13,000 military targets. In what was the biggest air campaign in a generation, around 500 combat aircraft executed around 250 sorties per day—10,000 sorties in 38 days, Wilsbach said.
American air bases in the Middle East went under “Alarm Red” conditions to take shelter, meaning there was an imminent threat of danger, 1,200 times. Wilsbach also said there were 48 airfield repairs and 420 “long lonely sweeps” to ensure that explosive ordnance was not left on the runway.
“That walk is exactly what the name suggests: one EOD technician, leaving a place of relative safety and approaching a suspected bomb or unexploded munition to render it safe for everyone else,” the chief said.
DUDE 44
Amid all these high-risk operations, the rescue of DUDE 44 in early April stood out as an example of the lengths the U.S. military was willing to go to save its service members.
In a recent interview with Air & Space Forces Magazine, Lt. Gen. Derek C. France, who was commander of Air Forces Central and the Combined Forces Air Component Commander for U.S. Central Command at the time of the mission and helped oversee the effort, said the rescue was one of his proudest moments in command.
“Watching 44 Bravo [the F-15E weapon systems officer] and getting the word that he was going to make it home and out of Iran with all the forces that were involved in that, knowing on Easter morning this guy was going to go see his family and call his wife for the first time in 48 hours was a high point, an emotional point for me having gone through that whole ordeal for the past 40-plus hours, and then recognized that we had got a win and got this guy back to safety,” France said.
For his part, Wilsbach singled out a particular battle manager—call sign “Peaches”—who coordinated the extraordinary search-and-rescue operation over 50 hours. To rescue the two-man crew, she and her team integrated the operations of 176 aircraft, including fighters, bombers, tankers, intelligence platforms, and special operations forces.
“Think about the complexity of that problem,” Wilsbach said. “Aircraft operating at different speeds, altitudes, fuel states, with different sensors, weapons, and responsibilities, while an adversary was actively trying to stop them.”
And that team was just part of the effort. Maintenance teams, Wilsbach said, generated additional fighters while tanker crews extended the force’s range and dwell time, and intelligence Airmen tracked threats.
“Every one of those Airmen was doing something different, yet all were contributing to the same mission,” Wilsbach said. That led to the 10 battlefield promotions, a rare occurrence when enlisted personnel are promoted for extraordinary performance of duties while serving in combat or under combat conditions.
“I had the distinct honor of promoting six of those heroes, ranging from staff sergeant to chief master sergeant, during a recent trip,’ Wilsbach said.
The dramatic rescue of the DUDE 44 crew began after an Iranian heat-seeking surface-to-air missile slammed into the two-seater fighter aircraft. Both crew members ejected. The pilot was rescued on the first day by a force that included A-10 Thunderbolt II attack aircraft, HC-130 Combat King IIs, HH-60W July Green II rescue helicopters, drones, and special warfare Airmen. That rescue operation was executed under close-range gunfire.
But the WSO, dubbed DUDE 44 Bravo, was not rescued for another day. He was injured in the fall, hitting the ground at a speed of 70 to 100 miles per hour after he struggled to unfurl a damaged parachute, according to an interview he gave to the CBS News program “60 Minutes.”
After landing five miles away from the pilot, DUDE 44 Bravo was suffering from a broken back, a broken arm, a broken shoulder, a sprained ankle, and cuts to his head and face. To elude capture, he scaled a 7,000-foot-tall ridgeline.
Airmen in Epic Fury
Wilsbach cited the work of Airmen across Epic Fury to emphasize his main directives for the service: be “ready to fight, built to endure, and integrated to win.”
The rescue of DUDE 44 was a prime example of integration, the chief said.
To illustrate readiness to fight, Wilsbach told the story of an unnamed base under attack from Iranian missiles.
“As missiles were inbound, Airmen sprinted toward bunkers,” Wilsbach said. “A missile struck nearby in a hangar, and the aircraft inside burst into flames. The bunker withstood the blast, but the force of the impact damaged the door so badly it wouldn’t open, trapping the Airmen inside.”
A security forces NCO used a pry bar to force the door partially open and spoke with the Airmen inside. But then the ejection seat on the burning aircraft ignited, “sending glass and metal fragments through the air,” Wilsbach said. At last, the Airmen were able to get the door open and run for cover. Finally, the door gave way, and the Airmen ran for cover.
Wilsbach also shared the story of an F-15E crew chief, Garrett, who stayed with the jets on the flight line until the last F-15E taxied and took off while others were running for cover. “When somebody later asked him why, his answer was simple: they needed those airplanes in the air,” Wilsbach said.
Hundreds of miles away, two Senior Airmen, Shanea and Nolan, tracked a swarm of enemy drones headed toward their base and, Wilbach said, achieved more than 10 surface-to-air kills.
Shanea and Nolan’s actions in particular show the need for the Air Force to advance point defense and make it a “core function of air and space power,” Wilsbach said; the Air Force can no longer be assured that it is safe from drone and missile threats, including at airfields in the United States.
“Don’t you think we ought to have them at every base?” Wilsbach said of a new field of Airmen specializing in point defense. “If every base is going to be threatened, we have to have somebody who knows how to defend it.
“If we had a more robust base defense, you know, perhaps those bases wouldn’t have been as damaged as they were,” Wilsbach added. “Look at Israel; they have a significantly layered, very robust defense of their country, and they didn’t take that many hits, very few, in fact. And that shows you what a good defensive system can do, which can help you to operate not quite with impunity, but almost, and you can just keep generating airpower, and your defensive systems take care of the incoming.”
To hammer home his point about endurance, Wilsbach told the story of a B-1 pilot, with the call sign Rocket, who coped with a harrowing refueling at night, in heavy clouds, and with jet fuel spraying across his cockpit windscreen.
The B-1 crew described the experience as “refueling by Braille,” Wilsbach said.
“A bomber pilot who couldn’t see depended on the tanker crew to guide them,” Wilsbach added, noting that the B-1 went on to complete a 34-hour mission.
Another example, the chief said, was an MQ-9 pilot, call sign Suit, who launched his drone while its airfield was under attack. The drone struck a target, then returned to base to conduct a damage assessment of the runway. That mission was one of many the MQ-9 conducted during Epic Fury, Wilsbach noted, with a remotely piloted aircraft striking more than 800 targets. It also played a key role in dynamic targeting and locations where the U.S. did not want to operate crewed aircraft. “Many more targets were hit because the MQ-9 found them and then passed them off to another platform,” Wilsbach said. “There’s a lot more than the 800 that they hit, and we were doing this in areas that were highly defended. And though we did decimate the Iranian Air Force and the Iranian Navy, and then we significantly attrited other capabilities that they have, it wasn’t easy. Iran’s not a pushover.”

articles.title: Iran dismisses US talks possibilities over Trump mixed messaging
articles.body:
A to Iranian official ruled out Tuesday any talks with the United States after President Donald Trump said he was open to resuming discussions on the Middle East war.
"Don't get distracted by the U.S. president's mixed signals – from 'no negotiations' to 'we're ready to talk,'" the secretary of Iran's Supreme National Security Council, Mohsen Rezaei, posted on X.
"The stakes around oil and the straits have changed. Damage control won't stop what's coming. No talks until Iran's conditions are met. Period!" he added.
Earlier Monday, Trump said he was open to holding talks with Iran, after weeks of saying it was too early to make a deal to end the war.
"The failing Nation of Iran wants to make a deal, quickly and badly. I will determine whether or not the U.S.A. will choose to engage – The concept of which we are open to," Trump said on his Truth Social network.
Iran has repeatedly listed demands including war reparations and the lifting of sanctions as preconditions for ending the war and its blockade on the Strait of Hormuz.
Meanwhile, Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) claimed Tuesday that it intercepted and "destroyed" two MQ-1 drones were near the Strait of Hormuz, marking the fourth such drone it says it has downed in recent days.
The IRGC said the drone was shot down east of the waterway by a newly deployed advanced air defense system operated by its Aerospace Force under Iran's integrated air defense network.
The Guards added that it intercepted another MQ-1 drone west of the Strait of Hormuz, without providing details on its operator or the exact location of the incident.
On Monday, they had also claimed to have "destroyed" another drone of the same type, according to Iranian state broadcaster IRIB.
In a separate development, Iran's Armed Forces General Staff issued a nationwide passive defense directive outlining preparations for three possible scenarios: the end of war, a cease-fire and full-scale war.
Maj. Gen. Ali Abdollahi, chief of staff of the Iranian Armed Forces and chairman of the country's Permanent Passive Defense Committee, issued the 10-article directive for Iran's 2026 Passive Defense Commemoration programs, according to Fars News Agency Tuesday.
Under the full-scale war scenario, large public gatherings and in-person events would be suspended, with activities instead focusing on operational preparedness, continuity of essential services, resource management, public assistance and coordination among relevant agencies.
In the event of a ceasefire without a definitive end to hostilities, the directive prioritizes public preparedness, vigilance against hybrid warfare and information security, while the end-of-war scenario provides for the full implementation of planned exercises, training and public programs.
The directive also calls for operational plans to be updated based on experiences from what it describes as Iran's "second and third imposed wars."
Iran has issued similar directives for its annual Passive Defense Commemoration in previous years, including 10-article instructions in 2024 and 2025 focusing on public preparedness and protecting critical infrastructure.
The latest directive, however, comes amid the ongoing war with the U.S. and explicitly sets out measures for three different conflict scenarios.
The U.S. and Israel launched large-scale attacks on Iran on Feb. 28, targeting government buildings, military sites, missile infrastructure, and air defenses. Iran responded with missile and drone attacks against Israel and U.S. bases across the region.
The conflict has since expanded across the region, while diplomatic efforts have sought to end the hostilities.
Before the current conflict, Iran and Israel had also fought a 12-day war in June 2025, which ended with a U.S.-backed cease-fire.

articles.title: Zelensky says Ukraine ready for 'de-escalatory steps'
articles.body:
Ukranian President Volodymyr Zelensky (AFP Photo)
President Volodymyr Zelensky has said that Ukraine is ready to de-escalate the war with Russia if its rival did the same, after U.S. President Donald Trump announced that the foes had agreed to end strikes on energy targets.
With international oil prices climbing again, Trump had at the weekend berated Ukraine’s attacks on Russian refineries, blaming them for causing a shortage in diesel fuel.
In one of his surprise social media posts, the U.S. leader announced on Sept. 14 that “Ukraine has agreed not to hit Russian Energy targets. Russia has agreed to do, likewise!”
Russia made no immediate comment. But in his nightly address, Zelensky highlighted “a strong proposal from the United States regarding a mutual halt to strikes on critical infrastructure.”
He added: “If this can become the first de-escalatory step, stopping Russian strikes on our critical infrastructure, and ours in response, then Ukraine is ready to support de-escalation.”
Zelensky said “we see that the Russians are feeling pressure because of our precise responses against Russia’s war economy.”
He noted that “so far no one has seen any genuine desire from Russia to move toward ending the war.”
“But if our American partners succeed in securing a real readiness from Russia to stop this war of destroying lives, and to do so sincerely and for the long term, Ukraine will make its own de-escalatory steps.”
Trump has insisted that the Russia-Ukraine war, and not the conflict with Iran, was driving up fuel costs for Americans who vote in crucial midterm elections in November.
A previous push by Trump for a ceasefire has been sidelined by the U.S.-Israeli conflict against Iran, now in its seventh month. U.S. envoys went to Moscow and Kiev earlier this month without announcing a breakthrough.
While Ukraine has hit refineries deep inside Russia, Zelensky has stepped up calls for allies to provide more anti-missile defenses as Russia intensifies its attacks.
Russian strikes on Ukraine’s rail network are worsening each week, the CEO of the state Ukrainian Railways operator told AFP on Sept. 14, after a strike hit a train frequently used by diplomats near the Polish border at the weekend.
“It’s growing exponentially. Each month, each week is generally worse than the previous one,” said Oleksandr Pertsovsky.
European Union countries on Sept. 14 delayed a deadline for prolonging sanctions on Russia after France pushed for billionaire Alisher Usmanov to be removed from a blacklist, diplomats said.
An EU list of almost 3,000 individuals and entities, which needs to be extended every six months, was set to expire by Sept. 16.
However, ambassadors from the 27 EU member states pushed back the deadline one week after the late efforts from Paris to remove 73-year-old Uzbek-Russian metals tycoon Usmanov drew opposition, the diplomats said.
The Financial Times reported, quoting people familiar with the issue, that France was making the push as part of a prisoner release deal involving French citizens held in Azerbaijan.

articles.title: Oil price could surge to $US150 as war engulfs major Middle East supply routes
articles.body:
Oil price could surge to $US150 as war engulfs major Middle East supply routes, analysts say
The Strait of Hormuz, the Red Sea and inland Saudi Arabia are now active war zones.
Yemen's Iran-aligned Houthis fired dozens of missiles and drones at a military air base in Khamis Mushait in southern Saudi Arabia overnight.
This latest escalation follows an attack on Thursday, which knocked out the Saudis' East-West pipeline.
The pipeline played a crucial role in easing the world's concerns about an impending global oil shortage.
For months, it had allowed oil tankers to bypass the blockaded Strait of Hormuz, a critical supply route for roughly 20 per cent of the world's oil supply.
Loading...
That was a major reason why oil prices were lower than they otherwise would be in the past few months.
The Houthis have also advanced rapidly in Yemen, capturing territory including Perim Island at the mouth of the Red Sea — a development which pushed oil prices above $US100 per barrel late last week.
And the British maritime security agency, UKMTO, reported on Sunday that another vessel had been struck by a projectile in the strait, forcing the crew to be evacuated as the ship caught on fire.
US in Middle East quagmire
The fighting between the Saudis and Houthis creates another problem for US President Donald Trump and other authorities trying to minimise the disruption to global oil supply.
Saudi Arabia has led a coalition battling the Houthis since 2015, but the conflict had largely quietened under a ceasefire in the past few years.
The fragile truce collapsed in July as Houthi strikes hit Abha Airport and the Houthis declared a naval blockade targeting Saudi-linked shipping.
Reuters reported that Washington has so far resisted Saudi requests for direct military intervention beyond intelligence support.
More pain at the pump
All those worrying developments have pushed the global benchmark, Brent crude, above $US107 per barrel today.
US West Texas Intermediate (WTI) crude also jumped to $US103 per barrel.
Tapis, which is Australia's regional benchmark crude price, is now trading at $US110 per barrel, up 46 per cent since July.
The price of Tapis effects the wholesale petrol price, or what service stations pay for fuel.
But the motoring group NRMA has told the ABC that the difference between the wholesale and retail price is currently non-existent.
This means the price of fuel at the bowser is likely to increase in coming weeks.
The average price of unleaded petrol, according to NRMA, has risen to $2.19 per litre, while the national average for diesel has lifted to $2.68.
"Unfortunately, the trajectory [for motorists] for the petrol price is up," NRMA spokesperson Peter Khoury said.
Mr Khoury, however, expects the price at the bowser to fall quickly if the Middle East conflict were to de-escalate.
But the message today from oil analysts is not encouraging on that front.
"The closure of the East‑West pipeline in Saudi Arabia following multiple attacks has materially altered the state of the oil market," Commonwealth Bank's lead mining and energy commodities strategist, Vivek Dhar wrote in a note.
"[It] means that instead of 40‑45 per cent of prewar flows through the Strait of Hormuz needed to keep global oil and refined product inventories unchanged, 65‑70 per cent of prewar flows are now required.
"The sizable shift almost single-handedly reflects the closure of the East‑West pipeline."
World running out of oil
Analysts now say the world is weeks away from returning to critically low levels of oil supply.
"Our low estimate that global markets had five to 11 weeks of global oil and refined product stockpiles is growing in likelihood," Mr Dhar said.
"This compares with our base case of 15‑20 weeks — where flows through the Strait of Hormuz were 30 per cent of prewar levels and global oil markets had the benefit of pipeline bypasses, subdued Chinese imports and rising non‑OPEC+ supply outside the Middle East."
He wrote that: "If inventory depletion is reached, we estimate that Brent oil futures may need to rise to [around] $US150 per barrel to force uncontrolled demand destruction (i.e. where high prices force lower demand) for emerging Asian economies."
That oil price would be even higher than what it was at the height of the global financial crisis.
In July 2008, Brent crude surged as high as $US147 per barrel.
"This price level is derived from the last time that emerging Asian economies saw uncontrolled demand destruction in 2008.
"With nonlinear rises in both oil and refined products now a real possibility, Iran has maximised its leverage against the US."
This will likely make it harder for Mr Trump to extract the United States out of its war with Iran, in a way that does not sound like defeat or capitulation.
Until then, the rest of the world is bearing the brunt of more expensive oil prices and higher cost of living.
