articles.title: Who Is Umar Kremlev? The Russian Businessman With Ties to Putin Who Partly Funded Trump Jr.’s Wedding Celebrations
articles.body:
A Russian businessman with ties to the country’s President Vladimir Putin footed the bill for celebrations following the wedding of President Donald Trump’s son, Donald Trump Jr., Trump Jr. and his wife, Bettina, have confirmed.
Oligarch Umar Kremlev’s contributions to the wedding festivities were first reported by ProPublica, which wrote that the Russian businessman spent hundreds of thousands of dollars to rent out a private island in the Bahamas and a fireworks show. The outlet reported that the guest list included roughly 50 guests, including family members, close friends, and Kremlev, who according to ProPublica was part of a larger group of Russian guests whose presence was a source of confusion for other attendees.
Trump Jr. and Bettina Trump shared a statement on social media in response to criticism over his financial involvement in the event, defending what she described as an “extraordinarily generous wedding gift from a friend” and denying any political motive behind Kremlev’s attendance.
“Our dear friend Umar very generously hosted two incredible nights of celebrations for us AFTER our wedding,” they wrote in a post on Bettina Trump’s Instagram on Monday in a caption that accompanied a series of photos from the evenings in question showing the couple partying with other guests, performances, and the beach-side venue. “It’s unfortunate that something so personal and happy can be recast as something political or sinister simply because of who someone is or where they come from. Friendship doesn’t require a political motive.”
The Trumps’ connection to a figure closely tied to the leadership in Russia—and his apparently lavish financial contribution to the wedding celebrations—has however drawn concerns from Democratic politicians and experts in ethics and intelligence, who have raised questions about what might be expected in return for the "gift" and warned that Russian intelligence services may seek to weaponize such a relationship.
Here’s what to know about Kremlev and his ties to Putin and the Trump family.
Who is Umar Kremlev?
Kremlev, 43, is a native of Tajikistan. He was previously known by his surname at birth, Lutfulloyev, which he changed to Kremlev in 2010 when he was in his late twenties, according to the independent Russian news organization Proekt. Prior to that name change, Kremlev was convicted of extortion in 2004 and battery in 2007.
He went on to join a notorious biker gang, the Night Wolves, not long after changing his name, according to Russian news reports. Outlets reported that during his time in the group, which was the first official biker community in the Union of Soviet Socialist Republics (USSR), Kremlev met Alexei Rubezhnoi, who currently leads Putin’s presidential security service. The Washington Post reported that Putin himself is considered an honorary member of the Night Wolves.
In 2015, Kremlev, who had boxed since he was a child, founded a company, Patriot, that promoted boxing matches. Two years later, he became the secretary general of the International Boxing Association (IBA) after a shake up led to Rubezhnoi becoming the chairman of its supervisory board. Rubezhnoi then nominated Kremlev to the secretary general position; from there, Kremlev went on to be elected as president of the IBA in 2020.
In 2024, Kremlev acquired Rolf, Russia’s largest car dealership group, which had previously been state-owned.
“These services,” Triplett says in reference to the Kremlin, “are exceptional at finding pain points and then and then manipulating them, and you can get people into difficult positions.”
What are Kremlev’s ties to Putin?
Kremlev has been connected with Putin for years, as has been documented through public appearances and business dealings.
During Kremlev’s time as IBA president, Gazprom, a state-owned energy company and one of the largest companies in Russia, became a financial backer of the boxing federation.
That same year, Kremlev stood alongside Putin during the opening of the International Boxing Center in Moscow.
Under Putin, many Russian government officials or oligarchs serve in supervisory positions for sports organizations in the country.
“Umar is guided by Putin. It was using the sport for soft political power,” an ex-IBA board member told ProPublica of Kremlev’s leadership of the organization. “It’s geopolitics. That it’s boxing is just happenstance.”
Following Kremlev’s acquisition of Rolf in 2024, meanwhile, Putin repealed the company’s federal ownership, which he had established through a presidential decree in 2023.
He was also honored by Putin with the Order of Friendship, according to the IBA, a state accolade that celebrates those who have helped to improve the Russian Federation in various sectors. And earlier this year, Kemlev accompanied Putin on a visit to China, according to Chinese state media. Kremlev’s press office told ProPublica in a statement that he was not part of the Russian President’s “official delegation” during the trip.
What are Kremlev’s ties to the Trump family?
Kremlev has been publicly linked to President Trump and Trump Jr. through the IBA in recent months. It’s unclear how else he may be connected with the Trump family.
After President Trump returned to the White House last year, Kremlev and the CEO of the boxing organization sent him an open letter congratulating him on his re-election and expressing the IBA’s “sincere gratitude for your strong and principled stance regarding the inadmissibility in the participation of ineligible athletes in women’s boxing competition,” in reference to Trump’s stance against the participation of transgender women in women’s sports.
The letter then nodded towards the 2028 Olympic Games, which will be hosted by the U.S. in Los Angeles, saying that the IBA looks ahead “with great optimism to the possibility of working together to make the Olympic movement great again, advance the sport of boxing and to champion the rights of athletes globally.”
Last September, Trump Jr. sat on a panel discussion hosted by the IBA in Istanbul, during which he also critiqued the participation of transgender women in women’s sports while onstage with Kremlev.
Kremlev’s press office said in its statement to ProPublica that he and Trump Jr. initially met “a couple years ago” and that the two men “have a friendly relationship.” It added that Kremlev “has never discussed political matters with any of his American friends and acquaintances,” Trump Jr. included.
A spokesperson for Trump Jr. told the New York Timesthat the two men bonded over boxing and hunting after meeting through a mutual friend, and that they are not in business with one another.
The President, who did not attend Trump Jr.’s wedding or the following celebrations, said in a statement provided to the Times on Monday that “I have no idea who Umar is, never heard of him, and he didn’t pay for Don and Bettina’s wedding, which took place at a totally different location, and on a different day.”
A spokeswoman for Eric Trump, Trump Jr.’s brother, meanwhile told the Times and ProPublica, “Eric has absolutely no clue who this person is.”
Intelligence experts raise concerns
“If the allegations are true, then it certainly reflects poor judgment on Donald Trump Jr.’s part,” Dan Hoffman, an intelligence expert with over 30 years of experience working in the Central Intelligence Agency (CIA), U.S. military, Department of State, and Department of Commerce, tells TIME. “It is highly unlikely Umar Kremlev would have any interaction with any member of the Trump family without the Kremlin knowing about it beforehand.”
Holden Triplett, who served nearly 15 years with the Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI) and was previously the Director for Counterintelligence at the National Security Council at the White House during Trump’s first Administration, says that any kind of relationship between an individual with ties to the President and someone linked to the Kremlin can pose a risk to the U.S.—though he says he doesn’t find the Trumps’ apparent relationship with Kremlev to be particularly alarming.
“Even the most above-board, non-threatening-nefarious relationship could be weaponized by intelligence services,” he tells TIME. “Russians commonly try to use, as a lot of intel agencies do, business relationships as a non-alarming way to establish connection with someone … It is one that the Russians have used with lots of, or attempts at least, with lots of other individuals in politics.”
This isn’t the first time Trump Jr. has drawn controversy over interactions related to Russia. During the 2016 presidential campaign, Trump Jr. met with a Russian lawyer who claimed she could provide information that would hurt his father’s Democratic opponent Hillary Clinton’s campaign. That meeting later became a point in the investigation special counsel Robert Mueller conducted into President Trump’s campaign and its ties to Russia, though Trump Jr. was never accused of wrongdoing in the probe.

articles.title: National Guard says it destroys Russian Tor-M1 air defense system worth $25 mln
articles.body:
Operators from the Black Sky unmanned aerial vehicle battalion of the Spartan brigade destroyed a Russian Tor-M1 anti-aircraft missile system valued at approximately $25 million, which the enemy had deployed deep in the rear near the occupied town of Vuhledar, commander of the Ukrainian National Guard Oleksandr Pivnenko said.
"Operators of the Black Sky unmanned aerial vehicle battalion of the Spartan brigade detected and destroyed a Tor-M1 anti-aircraft missile system that the enemy had deployed deep in the rear, near the occupied town of Vuhledar," Pivnenko said on Telegram on Monday.
According to him, the destroyed system is valued at approximately $25 million.
Tor-M1 is a mobile air defense system designed to protect troops and critical infrastructure from aircraft, missiles, and drones.
Pivnenko said the Russian military has been using such anti-aircraft missile systems in the war against Ukraine since 2014.

articles.title: Massive missile attack on Taganrog, 222 downed drones: Ukrainian strikes' aftermath
articles.body:
MOSCOW, September 15. /TASS/. Air defenses destroyed 222 Ukrainian drones over Russia overnight, the Defense Ministry reported.
Several residential buildings and one industrial facility were damaged in the Samara Region as a result of the drone attack. In addition, Rostov Region’s Taganrog was hit by a massive missile attack overnight. Warehouses belonging to the Ozon company and agricultural enterprises were damaged, as were the windows of residential buildings and an educational institution.
TASS has compiled the key details on the attacks’ aftermath.
Scale
- On-duty air defenses intercepted and destroyed 222 Ukrainian fixed-wing drones over Russia overnight, the Defense Ministry reported.
- According to the ministry, the drones were downed over the Oryol, Belgorod, Voronezh, Tula, Tambov, Bryansk, Rostov, Kursk, Lipetsk, Ryazan, Saratov, Samara, Kaluga, Ulyanovsk Regions, over Tatarstan and Crimea, as well as over the Black Sea.
- More than 30 drones and missiles were destroyed in Taganrog and nine districts of the Rostov Region, Governor Yury Slyusar reported on his Telegram channel.
- Sixteen drones were shot down over the Voronezh Region overnight, Governor Alexander Gusev said on his Max channel.
- Air defenses destroyed 11 drones over the Oryol Region in the past 24 hours, Governor Andrey Klychkov noted in a post on his Max channel.
Massive attack on Taganrog
- Taganrog came under a massive missile attack overnight, Rostov Region Governor Yury Slyusar said on his Telegram channel.
- According to preliminary reports, there were no fatalities or injuries.
- As a result of the missile attack, windows were damaged in two apartment buildings and three private homes, as well as at an educational institution, a commercial building, a gas pipeline, agricultural enterprise warehouses, a grocery store, and an Ozon warehouse, the governor noted.
- Emergency services are working at the scenes of the incidents.
- Three fires broke out as a result of a massive attack on Taganrog, Mayor Svetlana Kambulova reported on her Max channel.
- She specified that the windows of five apartment buildings and three private homes were damaged.
- Ozon later reported that the delivery hub of its logistics partner was evacuated due to the missile threat.
- No one was injured at the logistics partner’s warehouse.
- The company noted that the attack caused a fire in one section of the building; emergency services are on the scene.
- Ozon will redistribute the goods that were headed there to other facilities.
Other regions
- Several residential buildings and one industrial facility were damaged in the Samara Region due to a drone attack, Governor Vyacheslav Fyodorishchev said on his Max channel.
- There were no fatalities.
- An emergency response team is on the scene gathering information on the aftermath of the attack.
- Windows, roofs, and facades of four private homes were damaged by falling drone debris in the Voronezh Region, Governor Alexander Gusev reported on his Max channel.
- According to preliminary reports, there were no casualties.

articles.title: NATO fighter jets shoot down drone over Lithuania for the first time
articles.body:
NATO fighter jets shot down a drone that entered Lithuanian airspace overnight on September 15, marking the first time a drone has been downed in the country’s history, according to the Lithuanian public broadcaster LRT. The aircraft that carried out the strike were Italian fighter jets based at an air base in the city of Šiauliai.
The drone was detected in Lithuanian airspace around midnight, prompting authorities to declare an air raid alert in the Vilnius, Trakai, Elektrėnai, and Kaunas districts. It also disrupted airport operations, delaying several international flights.
The drone was shot down between Kaunas and Kaišiadorys, about 100 kilometers (62 miles) northwest of Vilnius.
According to preliminary information, the drone may have been carrying explosives. Authorities are still working to determine who owned it.
Lithuania has repeatedly declared air raid alerts in various parts of the country over drones entering its airspace — including Ukrainian drones that Russian electronic warfare systems knocked off course.

articles.title: There were 225 clashes at the front; Ukrainian forces eliminated 62 occupiers in the Pokrovsk direction, the General Staff reported.
articles.body:
There were 225 clashes at the front; Ukrainian forces eliminated 62 occupiers in the Pokrovsk direction, the General Staff reported.
Kyiv • UNN
Russian forces launched 225 attacks, carried out 55 airstrikes, and used more than 6,000 drones. In the Pokrovsk direction, 62 occupiers were destroyed.
Since the beginning of the day, there have been 225 combat engagements at the front; Ukrainian forces eliminated 62 occupiers in the Pokrovsk direction, with another 15 wounded, reports UNN, citing the General Staff’s update.
In total, since the beginning of this day, 225 combat engagements have taken place. The aggressor launched 55 air strikes using 190 guided aerial bombs, deployed 6,183 kamikaze drones for attacks, and carried out 1,724 shelling attacks on the positions of our troops and settlements
In the North-Slobozhanskyi and Kursk directions, two enemy assault operations have been recorded since the beginning of the day. The enemy carried out one air strike using one guided aerial bomb and shelled the positions of our troops and settlements 50 times.
In the South-Slobozhanskyi direction, the enemy attacked the positions of our units three times toward the settlements of Kozacha Lopan, Lyman and Obukhivka.
In the Kupiansk direction, the enemy attempted to improve its positions eight times, conducting assault operations toward Radkivka, Tyshchenkivka, Monachynivka and Kindrashivka. Five of these attacks are still ongoing.
Six attempts by the invaders to advance were repelled in the Lyman direction near the settlements of Novoiehorivka, Novoselivka, Drobysheve, Lyman and Yampil.
In the Sloviansk direction, the Defense Forces stopped seven attempts by the invaders to advance near the settlements of Ozerne, Kryva Luka and Mykolaivka. Two battles are ongoing.
In the Kramatorsk direction, the Russian invaders did not conduct any assault operations.
In the Kostiantynivka direction, the Defense Forces repelled 27 enemy assaults near the settlement of Kostiantynivka and toward Novoselivka, Illinivka, Dovha Balka, Rusyn Yar, Toretsk, Vilne and Stepove. Two attacks are ongoing.
The enemy carried out 22 attacks in the Pokrovsk direction. The occupiers attempted to advance toward the settlements of Hannivka, Bilytske, Dobropillia, Svitle, Matiiasheve, Serhiivka, Udachne, Molodetske and Novopidhorodne. One assault operation is still ongoing.
According to preliminary estimates, 62 occupiers were eliminated here today and 15 were wounded; six vehicles, a special-purpose piece of equipment, two UAV command posts, a fuel and lubricants depot, and 36 personnel shelters were destroyed. Five vehicles, nine UAV command posts and 123 personnel shelters were damaged. A total of 298 unmanned aerial vehicles of various types were destroyed or suppressed.
In the Oleksandrivka direction, the enemy did not conduct any assault operations.
In the Huliaipole direction, the Defense Forces repelled five enemy attacks near the settlements of Rizdvianka, Dobropillia and Charivne. One of these assaults is still ongoing.
In the Orikhiv direction, the enemy attempted to advance toward Shcherbaky and Stepnohirsk.
In the Prydniprovske direction, the occupiers did not conduct any offensive operations.
There were no significant changes in the situation in the other directions, the General Staff concluded.

articles.title: Estonia discusses joining French 'forward nuclear deterrence' project, prime minister says
articles.body:
PARIS, September 14. /TASS/. Estonia is in talks with France about joining Paris’ initiative on so-called forward nuclear deterrence, Estonian Prime Minister Kristen Michal told AFP.
Michal said that this was not an initiative that countries could simply join, as it required certain capabilities and a certain level of readiness. He noted that France was also helping ensure Estonia’s independence by deploying its troops there. He added that if nuclear cooperation could be deepened, it probably would be, and that Estonia was already under NATO’s nuclear umbrella.
Earlier on Monday, Finland decided to join the so-called forward nuclear deterrence project promoted by France. Finnish Defense Minister Antti Hakkanen said that the French initiative does not impose NATO-style collective defense obligations on participating countries.
In March, French President Emmanuel Macron said that Paris planned to move toward a "forward deterrence" initiative involving joint exercises with partner countries as well as the deployment of elements of France’s strategic forces in other European countries. He also announced plans to expand the country’s nuclear arsenal, while Paris no longer plans to disclose the exact number of warheads.

articles.title: Meink Reveals Space Force Has ‘On-Orbit Space Control Weapons’
articles.body:
NATIONAL HARBOR, Md.—Air Force Secretary Troy Meink revealed Sept. 14 the Space Force has “space control weapons” on orbit today—the Pentagon’s most direct acknowledgement to date that the U.S. is operating offensive capabilities in space.
“Today, we continue to ensure we remain ready to meet the challenge of evolving threats wherever they exist,” Meink said during the opening keynote at AFA’s Air, Space and Cyber Conference. “This is why the Space Force now has on-orbit space control weapons capable of defending the joint force against hostile adversary action.”
Meink’s explicit nod to U.S.-operated space weapons comes amid a concerted push to speak more openly about on-orbit threats and the Space Force’s ability to respond to them. China and Russia, in particular, continue to demonstrate aggressive maneuvers and are developing—and demonstrating—space weapons of their own. U.S. officials in recent years have discussed the need for “counter-space” capabilities and “space fires,” as well as the development of space-based interceptors designed to shoot down missile threats. And last December, President Donald Trump issued an executive order underlining the Space Force’s role in not only defending space assets, but also in the attack mission.
But Meink’s mention of existing on-orbit space weapons is a first. During a question and answer session following his speech, Meink said the acknowledgement was intentional and the phrasing “very well thought out.”
“It is critically important that we maintain our dominance, not only in the air but in space,” he said. “So, we’ve had to take steps to make sure that when we’re threatened, we can take care of that.”
Meink declined to discuss the capabilities in more detail during a briefing with reporters following his keynote—including whether the systems in question are kinetic or non-kinetic. He argued that while acknowledging the existence of U.S. space weapons in orbit may serve a deterrent function, “talking about the details of what we’re doing would actually not benefit that deterrence.”
“We’re not going to talk about the specifics of what we’re doing, whether we’ve tested, not tested, or anything else,” he said. “I would just say that the space environment is critical for military and economic security, and we need to make sure that the U.S. can operate freely there.”
Meink said the Space Force is working now to proliferate systems meant to help track and take out threats from space and highlighted two key efforts: the Space-Based Interceptor program and the Space-Based Air-Moving Target Indication constellation. Both are part of the Pentagon’s Golden Dome advanced missile defense shield.
On SBI, one of Golden Dome’s more ambitious technical lifts, Meink said the program has moved from “initial contract to flight-ready hardware” in under a year. The Space Force is leading a prize competition to evaluate the affordability and scalability of SBIs in increments and potentially field an initial capability by 2028.
Gen. Michael Guetlein, Golden Dome director, said in August the SBI contractor pool has completed the program’s first increment, called Gate One, which focused on solidifying a design and conducting component level testing. Guetlein said it appears all of the providers will move to Gate Two, where they will build a prototype. Those that progress to Gate Three must prove the capability works in space, and Gate Four providers must show their interceptors can be integrated with the broader Golden Dome architecture.
Another key Golden Dome contribution for the Space Force is its Space-Based AMTI program. While tracking airborne threats has long been a mission performed by aircraft, the Space Force is working with the National Reconnaissance Office to add satellites to the mix, with the goal of making the mission more resilient against adversaries’ anti-access/aerial denial systems.
The service awarded SpaceX a $4.2 billion contract in May to start building out the Space-Based AMTI constellation, and Meink said the first of those satellites will launch this month. The Space Force hasn’t disclosed how many spacecraft will initially launch or how many satellites the constellation will eventually feature.
“Taken together, these investments will help us adapt and scale the force for today and tomorrow’s threats,” Meink said.

articles.title: Lavrov: Had US not backed away from Anchorage, we would have lived without war for a year
articles.body:
Lavrov: Had US not backed away from Anchorage, we would have lived without war for a year
Russian Foreign Minister Sergei Lavrov has claimed that Russia "would have been living without war for a year" had the US "not backed away from the agreements" reached in August 2025 in Alaska.
Source: Lavrov at a round table on the Russia-Ukraine war, quoted by Russian propaganda agencies TASS, RIA Novosti and RBC
Quote from Lavrov: "If the Americans had not backed away from the Anchorage agreements, if Europe had not dragged those agreements out, we would have already been living without war for a year. That is a clear fact, so draw your own conclusions."
Details: Meanwhile, he reiterated the claim that Russia has allegedly "never refused negotiations."
"We have never refused negotiations. And all those negotiations that took place were halted not on our initiative. Therefore, if our colleagues are ready, I believe they can certainly be resumed. We have something to say," Lavrov stated.
He also insisted that Moscow has allegedly "never, not once, changed its position" since the start of the full-scale invasion of Ukraine and is supposedly "ready to seek compromises".
"Under this heading, we are prepared to search for reasonable compromises, but we have fundamentally not altered our objectives to guarantee our security, prevent NATO's presence on our borders, secure the legitimate rights of Russians and Russian-speaking people who have lived on these lands for centuries, and free them from the threats of Nazification, militarisation, and so forth," the Russian minister said.
He added that Moscow is allegedly prepared for both bilateral and trilateral negotiations.
However, the Russian official stated that the Russian Federation would not halt its aggression against Ukraine during any potential talks.
Background:
- On 15 June, Lavrov stated that Russia was awaiting a renewed visit from special envoys of the US president and wished to hear from them how America intends to implement the agreements on ending the Russian war against Ukraine, which were reached between Russian leader Vladimir Putin and Donald Trump in Anchorage in the summer of 2025.
- Following this, US Secretary of State Marco Rubio informed journalists that no agreements concerning Ukraine were made during the previous year's summit between US President Donald Trump and Russian leader Vladimir Putin.
- He subsequently added that the approach proposed by the Russians in Anchorage the previous year had failed, as it was unacceptable to Ukraine.
- Donald Trump and Vladimir Putin met on 15 August 2025 at a military base in Anchorage, Alaska. The meeting ended without any agreements being reached or any ceasefire in Ukraine being announced, despite claims of "significant progress".
- On 16 August 2025, after talks with Putin, Trump first spoke with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy and later with Zelenskyy and European leaders.
- Bloomberg reported that during the call with European leaders and Zelenskyy, Trump said Putin continued to demand the withdrawal of Ukrainian troops from the entire territory of Donetsk and Luhansk oblasts in Ukraine's east.

articles.title: U.S. Air Force AGM-190A missile goes from design to combat fast
articles.body:
- Air Force Special Operations Command said its AGM-190A Havoc Spear cruise missile passed a spring 2026 combat evaluation conducted with U.S. Africa Command.
- AFSOC and U.S. Special Operations Command developed the low-cost, modular missile through a cooperative research and development agreement in under three years.
The U.S. Air Force’s Havoc Spear cruise missile has passed a combat evaluation and is now cleared for broader use across special operations and conventional aircraft, Air Force Special Operations Command announced. The missile, officially designated the AGM-190A, was tested in a live operational setting during the spring of 2026.
AFSOC ran the evaluation in partnership with U.S. Africa Command, launching the missile from a C-130 aircraft in what the command described as a test configuration. Officials said the missile performed accurately and met AFSOC’s requirements for a small cruise missile, clearing the way for wider fielding.
Havoc Spear is built to be modular and mission-adaptable, meaning operators can configure it for different targets or effects, and the design is intended to keep production costs and timelines down compared with older cruise missile programs. AFSOC first revealed the missile’s name publicly in May 2026 at the Special Operations Forces Week conference in Tampa, Florida, where officials described it as capable of delivering long-range precision strikes with both kinetic and non-kinetic effects.
“Havoc Spear’s range and capabilities expands standoff options, giving commanders a versatile tool to neutralize threats without putting platforms or personnel in immediate danger,” said U.S. Air Force Lt. Gen. Mike Conley, AFSOC commander.
“It’s also not lost on us the value of being able to test a new weapon system in combat, and prove its success on the battlefield early on in the process,” Conley said.
The decision to run the evaluation through AFRICOM ties the missile’s early record to one of the U.S. military’s more active counterterrorism theaters. AFRICOM has spent years targeting militant networks across the continent, and Gen. Dagvin Anderson, the command’s chief, framed the test as part of that ongoing mission.
“We work every day to disrupt the networks that have made Africa the epicenter of global terrorism,” said U.S. Air Force Gen. Dagvin Anderson, AFRICOM commander.
“These successful operational assessments prove we will continue to bring the unique capabilities only the U.S. can provide in order to defend U.S. interests alongside our partners,” Anderson said.
Havoc Spear’s development path skipped much of the traditional acquisition process. U.S. Special Operations Command led the effort on AFSOC’s behalf, using a cooperative research and development agreement, or CRADA, with an industry partner rather than a standard program of record. That approach allowed the missile to move from design through combat testing in under three years, compared with the five to seven years such programs typically take.
“To outpace our adversaries, we can’t rely on traditional acquisition pipelines,” said U.S. Air Force Col. Robert Johnston, AFSOC director of strategic plans, programs and requirements.
“AFSOC is eager to explore more agile, lesser-known pathways to modernization to deepen industry partnerships, leverage calculated risks, and rapidly deliver capabilities to our warfighters,” Johnston said.
AFSOC has not disclosed the missile’s cost, its production rate, or which aircraft beyond the C-130 used in the AFRICOM evaluation will carry Havoc Spear as it moves toward wider use.

articles.title: Russian drones killed a man and injured eight in Kyiv, hitting two gas stations
articles.body:
Russian drones killed one man and injured eight people in Kyiv on the morning of 15 September, hitting two gas stations along with warehouses, a restaurant, and an office building, the National Police reported. The strikes came in a night-long wave of 200 drones that also hit Odesa Oblast in southern Ukraine.
What Russia hit in Kyiv
The first drone came down at a gas station in the Darnytskyi district shortly after 06:00, and more drones hit warehouses in the Obolonskyi district around the same time, the Kyiv Military Administration said. The strike critically wounded a man who was standing near the Darnytskyi station.
The attack resumed after 08:00. A drone struck a non-residential building in the Solomianskyi district, then a second gas station in the Holosiivskyi district, where heavy smoke rose over the site. Mayor Vitalii Klitschko reported the number of injured climbing through the morning, from two to four to eight, with two of them in serious condition. Emergency services put six of the eight in the Solomianskyi district, which took a second hit around 10:00.
The man hurt at the Darnytskyi station died in hospital at about 10:35. Beyond the two stations, police recorded damage to warehouses, a fast-food restaurant, and a business center.
The wave that carried them
Russia launched 200 strike drones from 18:00 on 14 September, the Air Force said: Shahed types including jet-powered ones, Gerberas, and Parodiya decoys, flown from Russia and occupied areas. Air defense downed or suppressed 187 of them by 08:00, with hits recorded at seven locations and debris falling at three more. The attack was still running when that count was published.
Russian forces hit Odesa Oblast at the same time. Russian forces struck residential buildings, logistics sites, and port and transport infrastructure, oblast head Oleh Kiper said, damaging roofs, facades, and windows of private houses along with dozens of garages and cars.
The same night, NATO fighters shot down a drone over Lithuania that had crossed from Belarus, and Ukrainian forces struck the Syzran refinery in Samara Oblast and a warehouse in Taganrog.
Why gas stations
Kyiv's filling stations have been under systematic attack since 10 September, when a drone came down at a station near a shopping mall. On 11 September, jet drones hit two Ukrnafta complexes on opposite banks of the city and returned to strike one of them a second time.
Unlike filling stations in the border oblasts, which Russia hits with cheap short-range drones, the Kyiv stations are being struck with its most expensive ones. Ukrainian stations are mostly struck with the Geran-4 Seeker, the variant fitted with machine-vision targeting, according military observer Oleksandr Kovalenko of Information Resistance.
More than 300 gas stations have been attacked across Ukraine since the current wave began, according to energy ministry data. The strikes have moved gradually from front-line oblasts deeper into the country, and about 80% of damaged stations return to work.

articles.title: Zelenskyy: Russia hits Ukraine's energy system, we retaliate
articles.body:
Zelenskyy: Russia hits Ukraine's energy system, we retaliate
President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has stressed that Russia continues to attack Ukraine's energy facilities, while the defence forces continue to respond with strikes on enterprises that support the aggressor state's defence industry.
Source: Zelenskyy on X (Twitter)
Quote: "Russia continues to attack our energy sector, regular logistics and critical infrastructure. And our responses to them for this are tangible.
There are new results from the defence forces of Ukraine regarding the refinery in Syzran. There was also a strike in Taganrog on a drone production facility, as well as on a drone preparation and launch site in Oryol Oblast. Targets were hit in the Black Sea as well.
I thank every one of our warriors for the effectiveness of our long-range sanctions!"
Background:
- On 14 September, US President Donald Trump said that Ukraine and Russia had supposedly agreed not to strike energy facilities.
- Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy commented in his evening address on 14 September on the US proposal for a mutual halt to strikes on critical infrastructure. "If this can become the first step towards de-escalation – a step involving an end to Russian strikes on our critical infrastructure and our strikes in response – then Ukraine is ready to support de-escalation," he said.
- The Financial Times, citing sources familiar with the matter, reported that talks on halting strikes on energy facilities have been under way for some time, but Kremlin leader Vladimir Putin does not want to reach an agreement before winter sets in.

articles.title: Sybiha: Russia recruiting agents in Germany for surveillance, sabotage; Europe must step up its countermeasures
articles.body:
Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andriy Sybiha called on European governments to step up efforts to counter Russian influence and strengthen cooperation in the field of counterintelligence following an investigation by German RTL journalist Angelique Geray, which revealed the recruitment of agents in Germany to carry out surveillance and sabotage missions.
"I am impressed by the courage of the German investigative journalist from RTL, Angelique Geray, who worked undercover to expose Russia's secret recruitment network in Germany," Sybiha said on X social media platform.
According to him, the investigation found that agents were recruited via Telegram in exchange for money to carry out surveillance and sabotage missions. The undercover journalist was also threatened.
Sybiha said the RTL investigation is not an isolated case but points to a broader pattern of Russian sabotage operations in Europe.
"Putin invests heavily in destabilising Germany and other European nations, especially ahead of elections," the foreign minister said.
He also said Russia's goal is to interfere in the internal affairs of European countries, manipulate public opinion, and exploit the most sensitive and controversial issues.
Sybiha called on European governments to take this threat seriously, expose Russian influence, and take urgent measures – including addressing Russia's diplomatic and cultural presence, imposing sanctions against accomplices, banning Russian propaganda, and strengthening cooperation in the field of counterintelligence.
"As one of the most experienced nations in countering Russian influence, Ukraine is ready to share its valuable experience upon our partners' request," Sybiha said.

articles.title: Denmark summoned Russia's ambassador after missiles were launched from a frigate at a military helicopter
articles.body:
Denmark summoned Russia's ambassador after missiles were launched from a frigate at a military helicopter
Kyiv • UNN
A Russian frigate fired two signal flares at a Danish AS-550 Fennec near Gedser. Denmark called the incident unacceptable but will not activate Article 4 or 5 of NATO.
Denmark’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs summoned the Russian ambassador in Copenhagen after an RF frigate fired two signal flares at a Danish military AS-550 Fennec helicopter. The ministry’s press service reported this on the social network "X," UNN reports.
Details
The Armed Forces report that one of the Air Force helicopters was fired upon with so-called signal flares during routine photography of a Russian frigate in the waters near Gedser. This is absolutely unacceptable. Therefore, the Russian ambassador was summoned for a conversation regarding the incident
Additionally
The incident occurred near Gedser. The AS-550 Fennec helicopter of the Danish Air Force came under attack. It was conducting routine photography of a Russian frigate that was in international waters.
Minister of Defense Jeppe Bruus stated that Denmark takes this "very seriously."
However, he noted that Denmark does not intend to activate Articles 4 or 5 of NATO, which provide for consultations among allies on security matters and stipulate that an attack on one Alliance country should be considered an attack on all allies.
Recall
A drone that flew into Lithuania from the territory of Belarus during the night was shot down by Italian NATO fighter jets. The drone’s wreckage has already been found, the Lithuanian Armed Forces report.

articles.title: Zelenskyy appoints Konstantyn Humeniuk as Commander of Ukraine’s Medical Forces
articles.body:
Zelenskyy appoints Konstantyn Humeniuk as Commander of Ukraine’s Medical Forces
President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has signed a decree appointing Konstantyn Humeniuk as Commander of the Medical Forces of the Armed Forces of Ukraine.
Source: decree on the President's Office website
Quote: "Humeniuk Konstantyn Vitaliiovych shall be appointed as Commander of the Medical Forces of the Armed Forces of Ukraine."
Details: In a previous decree, the president dismissed Anatolii Kazmirchuk from this position.
For reference: Konstantyn Humeniuk is a colonel in the medical service and an educator, and holds the academic degrees of Candidate of Medical Sciences and Doctor of Medical Sciences. He holds is an Honoured Doctor of Ukraine and is a recipient of the Borys Paton National Prize of Ukraine.
In May 2014, he served in the ATO The ATO or Anti-Terrorist Operation is a term used from 2014 to 2018 by the media, the government of Ukraine and the OSCE to identify combat actions in parts of Donetsk and Luhansk oblasts against Russian military forces and pro-Russian separatists. It was later renamed the Joint Forces Operation . In 2017, he became Chief Surgeon of the ATO, and from 2018 to 2019, he served as Chief Surgeon of the Joint Forces Operation. He has held the post of Chief Surgeon of the Armed Forces of Ukraine since 2019.
In May 2022, at a military mobile hospital in a frontline town near Bakhmut, he performed Ukraine's first advanced laparoscopic operation to remove a kidney on a patient suffering severe gunshot damage to the organ.
Background:
- Commander-in-Chief Mykhailo Drapatyi submitted a proposal to dismiss incumbent Medical Forces Commander Anatolii Kazmirchuk on 4 August.
- Anatolii Kazmirchuk holds the rank of major general of the medical service. He is a military physician, Doctor of Medical Sciences and professor. He was appointed Commander of the Medical Forces on 19 November 2023 by President Volodymyr Zelenskyy.
- In 2024, Anton Shevchuk – head of the medical service of the 82nd Separate Air Assault Brigade, who in July 2023 discovered Chinese-made tourniquets in his brigade and requested that the Medical Forces Command replace them – was reassigned to a lower position in another unit following a formal reprimand from his superiors.

articles.title: Ukraine confirms attack on Russian oil refinery and drone production facility
articles.body:
Ukraine confirms attack on Russian oil refinery and drone production facility
The General Staff of the Armed Forces of Ukraine has confirmed an attack on the Syzran Oil Refinery and the Atlant Aero facility in Russia.
Source: General Staff; Special Operations Forces on X (Twitter)
Details: On the night of 14-15 September, units of the defence forces of Ukraine hit Syzran Oil Refinery JSC in Samara Oblast in Russia and the Atlant Aero facility in the city of Taganrog in Russia's Rostov Oblast.
Direct hits followed by a fire were recorded on the territory of the Syzran Oil Refinery. The AVT-6 primary crude oil distillation unit and the tank farm were hit, the General Staff noted.
The Special Operations Forces (SOF) specified that this was a special operation conducted by their Deep Strike units in cooperation with the Unmanned Systems Forces (USF) and the Security Service of Ukraine (SSU).
Several SOF drones reached their targets. A large-scale fire broke out on the facility's territory, special forces operators confirmed.
Syzran Oil Refinery JSC is part of Rosneft Oil Company PJSC. The refinery's processing capacity is approximately 8.9 million tonnes of crude oil per year. The plant produces petrol, diesel and aviation fuel, as well as other petroleum products. The enterprise is involved in supplying the requirements of the Russian Armed Forces.
Meanwhile, explosions and a fire were recorded on the territory of the Atlant Aero company.
Atlant Aero specialises in the production of unmanned aerial vehicles and their components. In particular, the facility manufactures Molniya strike-surveillance UAVs and components for Orion UAVs. The enterprise is directly engaged in supplying the Russian Armed Forces with unmanned systems.

articles.title: Ukraine says ready for ‘de-escalatory steps’ if Russia does same
articles.body:
Ukraine says ready for ‘de-escalatory steps’ if Russia does same
Kyiv demands genuine commitment from Moscow as Trump claims deal to halt refinery and grid attacks
President Volodymyr Zelensky said on Monday that Ukraine was ready to de-escalate the war with Russia if its rival did the same, after US President Donald Trump announced that the foes had agreed to end strikes on energy targets.
With international oil prices climbing again, Trump had at the weekend berated Ukraine’s attacks on Russian refineries, blaming them for causing a shortage in diesel fuel.
In one of his surprise social media posts, the US leader announced on Monday that “Ukraine has agreed not to hit Russian Energy targets. Russia has agreed to do, likewise!”
Russia made no immediate comment. But in his daily address, Zelensky highlighted “a strong proposal from the United States regarding a mutual halt to strikes on critical infrastructure”.

articles.title: Petraeus: Ukraine needs interceptors, defense funds, partner sanctions against Russia to win
articles.body:
Retired U.S. Central Command Commander (2008–10), former CIA Director (2011–12), and Kyiv Security Forum (KSF) Security Council member David Petraeus has expressed the conviction that to achieve victory, Ukraine requires partners' assistance in overcoming several critical vulnerabilities, ranging from a shortage of interceptors to a defense budget deficit.
Petraeus called further pressure on the Russian Federation and the destruction of Russia's war economy the key to Ukraine's victory. He stated during a special meeting of the KSF Security Council in Kyiv that their task is to help Ukraine put Putin in a position where he realizes that the cessation of hostilities is just as necessary for him as it is for Ukraine. He noted that a sanctions package in the U.S. Congress has already been approved by an overwhelming majority in the Senate, which will complement the European Union's 22 rounds of sanctions. He added that if the European Commission can find a way to utilize the $300 billion in frozen Russian assets, that will also be a huge plus, and that other steps are needed to directly integrate Ukraine into the European military-industrial complex, which will benefit both Europe and Ukraine.
At the same time, the former commander highlighted Ukraine's impressive results at the front and deep in the enemy's rear. He noted that Ukrainian forces are currently monthly destroying or wounding a larger number of Russian soldiers than Russia mobilizes each month, that they are penetrating deeper into the enemy's logistics infrastructure, and that they are very effectively isolating Crimea by having destroyed 285 vessels that typically deliver goods, materials, and petroleum products there. He stated that in Crimea, electricity is disappearing, water is being cut off, and there will likely be no electricity this winter, making Crimea a burden for Putin.
Separately, Petraeus noted the unprecedented scaling of Ukrainian defense innovations, pointing out that instead of 8 million drones, there is a desire to manufacture 10 million this year.
The special meeting of the KSF Security Council was dedicated to the challenges awaiting Ukraine this winter. Its participants, in addition to Petraeus, included KSF Chairman and former Prime Minister (2014–16) Arseniy Yatsenyuk and former U.S. Special Representative for Ukraine (2017–19) Kurt Volker.

articles.title: NATO has begun discussing Article 5 because of Russian hybrid attacks, but Europe is still afraid of a tough response
articles.body:
NATO has begun discussing Article 5 because of Russian hybrid attacks, but Europe is still afraid of a tough response
Kyiv • UNN
NATO allies are considering a response to sabotage, cyberattacks, and strikes by the Russian Federation. There is currently no consensus on invoking Article 5.
Against the backdrop of intensifying Russian attacks on critical infrastructure and defense enterprises, European NATO countries are discussing possible response measures, but are avoiding radical steps due to the risk of direct escalation with Russia. Politico reports this, citing NATO diplomats and European officials, according to UNN.
Details
Among the options is a discussion of whether hybrid attacks or a combination of them could serve as grounds for invoking Article 5 of NATO on collective defense. The allies are also considering strengthening the protection of critical infrastructure.
If you continue doing this, we will not only have response options... we will also continue supporting Ukraine
NATO has so far decided to "keep calm"
According to a senior NATO diplomat, pressure on the Alliance is increasing following recent incidents, including a Russian drone strike on a train near the Polish-Ukrainian border. However, he described the current strategy as "keeping calm and continuing... to support Ukraine."
Politico notes that concern is growing in Europe over sabotage, cyberattacks, and other actions that remain below the threshold of conventional war.
According to the publication, NATO does not yet have an official plan for responding to such incidents. Some allies are informally proposing defining a threshold beyond which a series of hybrid attacks could raise the question of invoking Article 5, but there is currently no consensus on this within the Alliance.

articles.title: Russia Recruits More Than 28,000 Foreign Nationals for War in Ukraine
articles.body:
- Category
- War in Ukraine
Russia Recruits More Than 28,000 Foreign Nationals for War in Ukraine
Russia has recruited more than 28,000 foreign nationals to join its war against Ukraine, including a substantial number of people from African countries, according to Ukraine’s Defense Intelligence (HUR) chief Oleh Ivashchenko.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
In an interview with The Times, Ivashchenko said Ukrainian intelligence is working to disrupt Moscow’s efforts to recruit fighters abroad.
“We’re working to stop this, by passing information to the relevant security and intelligence services. We also conduct non-kinetic operations to inform the population in the relevant countries,” Ivashchenko said.
Beyond recruiting foreign nationals, Russia continues to receive military assistance from North Korea. HUR estimates that approximately 8,000 North Korean troops are currently deployed in Russia’s Kursk region, with their number potentially rising to around 50,000.
Russia’s reliance on foreign manpower extends across multiple regions. In an earlier interview with Ukrinform on September 7, Ivashchenko said Moscow was recruiting nationals from more than 40 countries as it seeks both to replenish battlefield losses and expand its forces for potential future military objectives.
“Today, Russia is using foreign nationals from more than 40 countries, including countries in Central Asia, Africa, and Latin America. They are primarily deployed in assault units. In intercepted communications, the Russians themselves call them ‘allies’ and often send them ahead of their own troops,” he stated.
Overall, Ukraine’s Foreign Ministry estimates that Russia has recruited at least 2,982 nationals from 37 African countries into its armed forces, with approximately 486 reportedly killed in the war against Ukraine.

articles.title: Has a Chinese DF missile been used for the first time in the Middle East?
articles.body:
Has a Chinese DF missile been used for the first time in the Middle East?
Video of a DF-15A rocket motor in Marib hints at secret arms deliveries as Saudi-Houthi fighting escalates
Video clips circulating on social media in the past week showed debris from the booster stage of a short-range ballistic missile with “DF-15A” written on its side found in the Raghwan district of Marib governorate, about 170km (105 miles) by road from the Yemeni capital, Sanaa.
The same images were carried uncensored by multiple Chinese online news outlets.
The discovery marks the first time the DF-15A missile, and more broadly the Dongfeng missile series, has been found operating in the Middle East. There are no previous confirmed reports of its export to Middle Eastern entities, suggesting the Chinese-made missile may have been delivered covertly to the region.
The DF-15A is the advanced variant of the Chinese DF-15 short-range ballistic missile, a series with a range of up to 900km. While the DF-15 series is classified as a single-stage solid-propellant missile system, the recovered hardware appears to correspond to the large solid-rocket motor casing used during the initial boost phase of flight.

articles.title: What the closure of Saudi Arabia's East-West pipeline could mean for oil flows
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
What the closure of Saudi Arabia's East-West pipeline could mean for oil flows
Saudi Arabia's closure of a major oil pipeline after a recent attack is raising fears that global energy markets in crisis because of the war with Iran could face even starker shortages, pushing prices higher for fuel and other essentials.
The largest oil producer in the Middle East closed its East-West pipeline on Friday after the attack, which it blamed on drones from Iranian-backed militias in Iraq. Two regional officials told The Associated Press that repairs could take three to five weeks.
The pipeline is crucial to getting some crude out of the Middle East by shipping it to the Red Sea rather than through the Strait of Hormuz, the narrow waterway through which roughly a fifth of the world’s oil supply passed before the US and Israel attacked Iran in February.
Yemen's Iran-backed Houthis have seized islands along key Red Sea shipping routes, further threatening Saudi exports. And while several limited alternatives remain, including trickles of tanker traffic in Hormuz, experts warn more supply shocks and higher prices straining households could pile up. Brent crude, the international standard, traded at more than $105 a barrel Monday.
Here's what we know:
What is the East-West pipeline? 
Saudi Arabia's East-West pipeline stretches some 1,200 kilometers (746 miles) across the desert nation—carrying oil from a processing facility near the Gulf westward to the Red Sea. There, crude is typically loaded onto tankers that head north towards Europe via the Suez Canal or south through the Bab al-Mandeb Strait, on the way to Asia.
The pipeline was built in the 1980s amid fears that Tehran would disrupt shipping through Hormuz during the Iran-Iraq war. And for the first six months of the current war, it was crucial to keeping at least some oil flowing out of the Middle East while most tanker traffic in Hormuz remained at a standstill.
Rystad Energy said Monday that an average 2.6 million to 4 million barrels of oil a day moved through the pipeline and out of the Red Sea port of Yanbu since late August—a volume it said is now at risk of "disappearing from the market."
Four million barrels per day is about 4% of the global oil supply, according to the International Energy Agency. Saudi Arabia produced nearly 10 million barrels of oil a day in September 2025, but was down to 6 million barrels per day in August, the IEA said.
Janiv Shah, vice president of oil markets for Rystad Energy, noted the recent jump in Brent prices proves the market is already responding to "a significant loss of supply." Saudi inventories could sustain exports in the coming days, but that could “change quickly," Shah added.
Where oil flows from the Middle East stand now 
The Strait of Hormuz is still top of mind. Before the war, about 20 million barrels passed through Hormuz each day.
Some tankers are again traversing the strait, but traffic is well below what it once was. Maritime data company Lloyd's List Intelligence counted 90 transits in the first week of September. Before the war, about 130 ships passed through daily.
The Houthis have also tightened their hold on the Bab al-Mandeb Strait, a vital passage for the southern Red Sea. Analysts at Melius Research estimated that about 3 million barrels of oil a day were moving through Bab al-Mandeb in early September, but noted Monday that "it's likely zero now."
Because of Houthi attacks, most Saudi traffic from Yanbu went north to the Mediterranean, either via the Suez Canal or Egypt's SUMED pipeline. But the Houthis have also begun targeting Saudi shipping in the north.
Salvatore Mercogliano, a professor of maritime history at Campbell University in North Carolina, noted that at least Hormuz is still on the table.
"If this (East-West pipeline) was the only method for Saudi Arabia to get their oil out it would be absolutely cataclysmic," he said. “But since the Hormuz route has opened back up—not completely but opened up some—it's not the death knell for Saudi Arabia. They're getting oil out."
Prices keep climbing 
Supply squeezes have led to soaring prices worldwide. And analysts warn that the latest disruptions could bring even more pain for consumers in the coming weeks and months.
One of the most immediate consequences is the cost of fuel and household energy bills. Countries in Asia and Africa, which rely more heavily on imports from the Middle East, have experienced some of the starkest shocks.
In Nigeria, for example, diesel prices are now 92% higher than they were in late February, and gasoline prices are up nearly 61%, according to energy tracker Global Petrol Prices. Countries including Indonesia (diesel up 87% and gas up 38%) and Lebanon (diesel up 80% and gas up 46%) have also seen steep spikes.
In the US, the price per gallon of regular gasoline was nearly $4.32 on average Monday, up almost 45% from the $2.98 seen before the war, according to motor club AAA. Diesel hit another all-time high (without accounting for inflation) of $6.23 per gallon on average Monday, up nearly 66% from the start of the war.
The cost of diesel, in particular, makes its way into other goods because the fuel is used for long-haul trucks and other delivery networks, as well as farm equipment.
"An inflationary spillover is likely," warned Melius Research analysts on Monday, pointing to the war's squeeze on essentials like fertiliser as well as energy sources. "The diesel crunch is also coming ahead of the US harvesting and heating season."

articles.title: F-35 Readiness Surged in Epic Fury; Now Pentagon and Lockheed Eye Broader Gains
articles.body:
NATIONAL HARBOR, Md.—For years, sustainment challenges and spare parts shortages have hindered the F-35 Joint Strike Fighter’s readiness. But the Air Force’s experience flying F-35s heavily in operations against Iran have showed what the jet can be capable of, if maintainers get all the supplies and support they need.
Brig. Gen. Brian Laidlaw, director of operations for Air Combat Command, said during a Sept. 14 panel discussion at AFA’s Air Space & Cyber conference that the F-35 “absolutely proved itself” during Operation Epic Fury—and keeping a steady flow of spare parts was critical.
“When properly resourced, we showed without a doubt how well this airplane can perform in combat,” Laidlaw said. “When we send our aircraft into harm’s way and they go downrange, they enjoy a higher priority for spare parts and all the things that the logistics trail can get to them. What we saw is how remarkably well the F-35 airplane withstood and maintained really high mission capable rates over a long period of time in the toughest of combat situations.”
The challenge now facing the Air Force, F-35 prime contractor Lockheed Martin, and other parts of the Joint Strike Fighter enterprise: how to keep that level of readiness up, even for aircraft not on the front lines of combat?
A Government Accountability Office report released this June made clear the F-35’s readiness woes are still an issue—just one in four U.S. jets were considered “fully mission capable,” or ready to carry out all their missions at any given time, in fiscal 2025. The Air Force’s full mission capability rate was highest of all U.S. services at 28.5 percent, while the Navy and Marine Corps’ F-35s ranged between 15.3 to 22 percent.
The GAO report cited multiple problems, including spare parts shortages and the military’s decision years ago to prioritize buying more F-35s early in the program’s life cycle instead of investing in critical depot and repair capability. That choice led to a historic underinvestment in sustainment, GAO officials said, that has resulted in a sustainment system that can’t fully support the F-35 fleet.
Yet recent development have shown the Air Force’s larger sustainment enterprise kicking into high gear. In his keynote address Sept. 14, Air Force Secretary Troy Meink continued to harp on the importance of readiness, a frequent theme in his tenure, and said targeted campaigns such as the North Star Readiness Campaign for bombers is helping improve aircraft availability.
During Operation Epic Fury, Meink said, sustainment centers surged procurement of parts by nearly 120 percent to keep aircraft flying. Contractors have also spent billions of their own dollars to stock up on parts military aircraft need, he said.
“The result: our fleet health is showing meaningful progress,” Meink said. “And with Congress’ support, we’ll follow that up with record-high spare parts investment in the next year, and years to come.”
For the F-35 in particular, Dina Halvorsen, vice president of F-35 global sustainment at Lockheed Martin, pointed to several steps the company and the U.S. military have taken to turn around the fighter’s lagging availability in a briefing with reporters at the conference.
In early 2024, Halvorsen said, Lockheed and the F-35 Joint Program Office teamed up to create a “joint model” that spelled out what kind of parts, and how many, would be needed to make F-35s 80 percent mission capable—able to carry out at least one mission—and 65 percent full mission capable.
“It had become very clear that jointly, we [Lockheed and the military] had underinvested in sustainment for the number of jets that we had and flight hours that we wanted to fly,” Halvorsen said.
The team spent about 18 months working on that model, she said, and when it was ready in late summer 2025,, Lockheed made its first $1 billion investment in spare parts.
“We knew what parts were needed, and we didn’t want to wait another year, which is the cycle it would take to get through a congressional budget and get that funding aligned,” Halvorsen said.
Buying that first tranche of spare parts cut out nine or 10 months of lead time, Halvorsen said—and started to position the F-35 for the intense pace of operations that 2026 would bring. Flight hours on all F-35s worldwide are up 25 percent year over year, Halvorsen said, which she said is “putting even more stress on the system.”
But that major infusion of cash didn’t solve everything.
“With all the work we did to buy those initial parts, we realized there were some capacity gaps within the supply chain,” Halvorsen said. “So I could go buy parts, but I wasn’t going to get them in time.”
So Lockheed invested another $1 billion to try to fill that shortfall, Halvorsen said, and figure out what critical components it needed to invest in. That led to a second tranche of spare parts purchases, she said.
In July, the F-35 Joint Program Office awarded Lockheed a record $1.6 billion contract for critical spare parts, which Halvorsen said “liquidated” some of the first tranche of parts Lockheed had bought.
Halvorsen also said Lockheed plans to do more advanced procurement of spare parts to be ready for 2027 and further shrink supply times. That kind of buy-ahead is needed to fully engage the vast array of subcontractors that make F-35 parts, she said—and shows why multiyear purchase agreements for both production and sustainment are so important for the fighter.
“We’re going to keep the supply chain engaged, because to build the capacity, you have to have the demand,” Halvorsen said. “So if you don’t put your total demand into the supply chain, they will never build to the capacity that you need. … We think it’ll drive down overall cost, because if you buy year-to-year, you’re certainly paying for that sort of thing.”

articles.title: Russia Could Be Preparing Serious Strikes on Poland in Coming Weeks and Months, Tusk Warns
articles.body:
- Category
- War in Ukraine
Russia Could Be Preparing Serious Strikes on Poland in Coming Weeks and Months, Tusk Warns
Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk warned that Russia’s escalating actions could increasingly affect Poland in the coming weeks and months, as Moscow intensifies attacks near the country’s borders.
Speaking at a briefing at Poland’s Government Security Center on September 13, Tusk said recent developments showed that Russian escalation was becoming increasingly apparent and moving closer to Polish territory, according to Polish broadcaster RMF24.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
“Russia’s escalation is becoming a reality, and examples of it are getting closer and closer to our border,” Tusk said. “We must be prepared for a joint response if necessary.”c
Tusk also pointed to Russia’s latest attacks on Ukraine as evidence that Moscow is deploying increasingly dangerous weapons, specifically highlighting the growing use of jet-powered drones.
“The attacks last night demonstrate that the Russians are ready to use more dangerous equipment. I mean jet-powered drones […] Obviously, Ukraine, which is very well prepared to defend against drones, is also unable to counter them with 100% effectiveness,” he said.
Polish Deputy Defense Minister Cezary Tomczyk, who also attended the briefing, said 13 strikes were recorded in western regions of Ukraine during the Russian drone attack on September 13.
Against this backdrop, Tusk called for an assessment of Poland’s readiness to respond to potential drone-related threats, including operations that could disrupt critical infrastructure and transportation networks.
“I will therefore also be waiting for information on how prepared we are for the possible use of drones and related attempts to disrupt our operations, on the railway or elsewhere. I do not rule out that such situations could also occur here,” Tusk said.
His warning came as the September 13 Russian attack reached areas immediately bordering Poland. A Russian drone struck the locomotive of a Kyiv-Warsaw passenger train in Ukraine’s Volyn region, approximately two kilometers from the Polish border.
State railway operator Ukrzaliznytsia reported that no one was injured, adding that a monitoring team had warned the train crew of the threat in advance.
The same attack also damaged infrastructure near the Yahodyn-Dorohusk international border crossing, one of the main road connections between Ukraine and Poland.

articles.title: Gulf states cancel meeting with Iran; Houthis attack Saudi Arabia
articles.body:
Arab nations have cancelled a meeting with Iranian representatives scheduled for the 14th of September, and the Houthi group in Yemen has once again launched attacks on Saudi Arabia, further threatening the flow of global oil supplies, reports Reuters.
The Iran-linked Houthis in Yemen reported launching missile and drone strikes against a Saudi air force base in Khamis Mushait, near the border. Aircraft hangars, runways, and ammunition depots were hit. The attack was reportedly in response to hundreds of strikes launched by Saudi Arabia against Yemen in recent days.
Saudi officials issued a brief emergency alert in cities that have previously faced Houthi attacks. Last week, the Houthis managed to capture an island near the Bab el-Mandeb Strait. In a separate attack—which Riyadh blames on Iranian-backed militants from Iraq—Saudi Arabia’s West-East oil pipeline was damaged; this pipeline served as a key route for exporting oil from the Middle East without using the Strait of Hormuz. On the 14th of September, crude oil prices rose by more than 3%, while the price of diesel in the US—a politically sensitive commodity—climbed to an all-time high of 6.23 dollars per gallon. Oil traders have noted that the pipeline shutdown could halt approximately 4% of global oil exports. Satellite imagery shows that the damaged sections of the pipeline have caught fire. Riyadh has not yet offered a forecast regarding how long the pipeline might remain closed.
A meeting between representatives from Iran and Persian Gulf states was scheduled for the 14th of September
in Oman to discuss reopening the Strait of Hormuz to traffic; the strait has been effectively closed since the last day of February. However, the meeting was cancelled. Iran stated that this was done at the request of Saudi Arabia.
Meanwhile, Iran has released a list of 77 vessels alleged to have violated protocols for navigating the Strait of Hormuz. These vessels will henceforth be barred from crossing the strait and will face penalties; they may also be detained or confiscated.
The escalation of hostilities in Yemen presents a dilemma for Washington. It faces pressure to assist its allies in Saudi Arabia but is reluctant to expand a conflict that is already proving extremely costly for the US. Saudi Arabia has been leading a coalition fighting the Houthis for over a decade. A truce had been in effect for the past couple of years, but hostilities have now resumed. Thousands of Yemenis have moved from the coast to the interior.
