articles.title: A century ago, bright red trousers made soldiers easy targets. Ukraine’s ex-army chief says the West is wearing them again
articles.body:
Ukraine's former top commander has a warning for anyone betting that new gadgets will win the war, he wrote in a column for Ukrainska Pravda. Valerii Zaluzhnyi, the country's Commander-in-Chief until 2024 and now its ambassador to the UK, argues 2026 is a war of technologies and, no less, of the strategies and doctrines that must keep pace with them. Bolting modern tech onto an old Soviet playbook, he says, drove mobilization into a dead end.
A year ago, Zaluzhnyi warned that Ukraine would need thousands of counter-drone systems and mass drone production to cope with the growing role of UAVs in war. A year later, those capabilities still aren't there at the scale he called for, mobilization has hit the dead end he now describes, and the four measures he proposed have not kept pace with how quickly drones are spreading.
Drones are already cheap, widespread, and shaping the war, and the front has gone static, Zaluzhnyi writes, while Russian strikes keep reaching railways and fuel stations far behind it.
This is no longer a drone war
The drones filling headlines no longer exist on their own, Zaluzhnyi writes. They have evolved into more familiar weapon types, cheaper and more effective—anyone still treating drones as a stand-alone class is about three years behind. Fixating on individual gadgets, he argues, misses the real contest: strategy and doctrine.
He reaches back to World War I for the danger he sees, running the line from Verdun and the Somme to Robotyne and Bakhmut. Before that war, soldiers in one army marched in bright red trousers that were supposed to help against repeating rifles, machine guns, and long-range artillery, and later against tanks and aircraft.
Today's faith in old security guarantees, he warns, is that same proud symbol worn onto a modern battlefield.
"The red trousers taught them nothing," he writes of those still moving tanks and artillery toward the fight by yesterday's logic.
New weapons, old strategy
The war has surrendered itself to marketers and wheeler-dealers, Zaluzhnyi writes—people who, without understanding or strategy, stoke it for quick profit while flaunting the pace of technological progress. Trying to retake land with Soviet methods and new weapons drove mobilization into a dead end, and fewer and fewer people were willing to take the one chance it offered.
"Damn marketing that kills," he adds.
The way out, he argues, is to treat technology as a new weapon, build tactics around it, and only then reshape the force.
That is what he calls doctrine, built through resource and technological alliances into a strategy for victory. Ukraine and Russia, he writes, have become real-time testing grounds.
What he warned a year ago
In September 2025, Zaluzhnyi named the four fights Ukraine had to win to survive mass drone warfare: counter-drone systems at scale, state-level drone production, integrated battlefield networks, and channeling tech talent into defense industries.
The counter-drone systems he put first are still short of the scale he warned Ukraine would need. Mobilization, he writes, has hit a dead end, and marketers—not the doctrine he calls for—are setting the pace.

articles.title: Yemen's Taiz prepares for siege as residents take up arms
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
Yemen's Taiz sees growing popular mobilisation amid fears of Houthi siege
A state of general alert and mobilisation has been declared in Yemen's Taiz province amid escalating fighting and fears that the Houthis could impose a full siege on the province.
The move comes amid continued fighting on Yemen's western coast, with clashes reported in the past 24 hours to the east, west and south of Taiz.
The past hours have seen fierce clashes around the air defence axis and western and southern Taiz, while government forces have thwarted Houthi infiltration attempts in Jabal Habashi and Bani Omar.
Government aircraft also carried out strikes targeting Houthi reinforcements and vehicles on Al-Siteen road and around Al-Kadaha and Al-Ahkloom. The fighting was accompanied by reciprocal artillery fire and repeated closures of the eastern Al-Qasr crossing following Houthi shelling.
Fears of a full siege
Taiz has significant political and geographical importance and is considered the main obstacle to Houthi expansion. The group has been applying pressure towards the province's eastern and southern flanks, seeking to exploit changes in the military map to tighten its grip.
The Houthis are seeking to impose a complete siege by taking control of the only southern route linking Taiz with the interim capital Aden and other provinces controlled by the internationally recognised government.
Such a move would close the last outlet for the movement of people and the flow of essential goods, food and medicine into the province.
Around four million people live in Taiz and residents fear that a siege would worsen already severe humanitarian and economic conditions.
The threat has also revived memories of the early years of the war, prompting residents and local groups to prepare for a possible siege rather than wait for political solutions.
General mobilisation declared
The "Supreme Council of Popular Resistance" in Taiz, a group allied with the government, has called for general mobilisation across all government-held provinces and districts and urged people to unite to defend them.
It also called on the Presidential Leadership Council to assume its responsibilities and use all available resources to support efforts to restore the state.
The mobilisation has extended across Taiz's districts, with meetings bringing together local notables and political and security officials in an effort to overcome internal divisions and strengthen the province's internal front.
The Emergency Committee in Mishr'a and Hadnan district held an expanded meeting attended by Taiz deputy governor for defence and security affairs Major General Abdul Karim Al-Sabri and deputy governor and head of the mobilisation and support committee Sheikh Aref Jamel.
The meeting stressed the seriousness of the situation and the need to raise readiness to the highest levels.
Taiz Governor Nabil Shamsan also discussed preparations with dignitaries from Al-Shamayatayn district, stressing the importance of strengthening internal unity. He praised Saudi Arabia's continued support and said the province's security was a top priority requiring the coordination of popular and official efforts through a comprehensive emergency plan.
"Front support committees" have also been formed to provide logistical support, organise general mobilisation and facilitate voluntary recruitment to reinforce the armed forces.
Mohammed Al-Ezzi, secretary of the Nasserist Unionist People's Organisation in Mishr'a and Hadnan district, told The New Arab that there was an unprecedented national consensus among Taiz's political and social groups in support of armed popular mobilisation alongside the national army.
Al-Ezzi said the mobilisation reflected growing awareness of the threat posed by the Houthis.
"The Houthi militias are targeting Taiz, its land and its people, because of its strategic position at the heart of the national project, as the maker of revolutions, the pillar of the republic, and the state's line of defence against separatist projects," he said.
He added that the Houthis were seeking to undermine the republican system by subjugating Taiz and taking revenge on the province because it was "the first to reject the [2014 Houthi] coup, and it continues to carry the banner of defending the state".
Al-Ezzi said political forces and parties in Taiz had succeeded in "turning the page on internal differences and unifying the compass".
He said the groups understood that "there is no survival for groups or individuals except in the presence of the state, and there is no meaning to any political projects if the militia succeeds in bringing down Taiz".
He added that "defending the republican system and the state is a matter of national consensus and a foundation of the collective consciousness of all the province's residents".
Residents prepare for possible siege
Journalist Wisam Mohammed told The New Arab that calls for popular mobilisation might initially appear unlikely to attract a major response because of political divisions, the legacy of corruption and government failures, and the lack of services.
However, he said the Houthis' control of Mokha and Bab al-Mandab, their approach towards the main roads linking Taiz to Aden and Lahj, and threats to impose a siege had pushed political and social groups to put their differences aside.
"The nature of the conflict in Taiz is political and civilian, which makes it dissolve when faced with real danger," Mohammed said, adding that the military and political leadership needed to develop mechanisms to organise and absorb the growing popular mobilisation.
He said current conditions were pushing more people to participate in defence because of accumulated suffering and lessons from the war, as well as growing awareness of the danger posed by a possible siege.
Mohammed also pointed to a significant demographic change, saying the population of Taiz city was now three times what it was at the beginning of the war because of the return of residents to the city and surrounding rural areas.
The threat of a siege has also affected living conditions, with prices of basic goods and fuel rising as fears grow over a possible tightening of the cordon.
Residents have also expressed concern about disruptions to supply lines and transport along alternative roads, while prices of individual weapons and equipment have risen amid increased demand.
Arms and ammunition markets across Taiz have seen a notable increase in demand, with residents buying personal weapons and ammunition at their own expense.
During a field visit to markets in the province, The New Arab observed a rush to buy weapons and individual equipment. Some residents were selling family gold and jewellery to raise money to buy weapons.
Mahyoub Saif, a 60-year-old resident interviewed by The New Arab in the market, said residents did not want to repeat what happened in 2015.
"We do not want to repeat the mistakes of 2015. We were civilians and did not know the weapons or care about them. When we were forced to fight, five fighters would take turns using one Kalashnikov. Today, every individual must have his own weapon," he said.
"We know very well that the Houthis want to invade Taiz and bring it to its knees, so I gathered what remained of the gold belonging to my wife and daughters, sold it and bought two Kalashnikovs so that I would be ready," he added.

articles.title: Price of Epic Fury: Iran war’s toll on US bases, weapons and more
articles.body:
Price of Epic Fury: Iran war’s toll on US bases, weapons and more
Pentagon inspector general offers an official accounting of the war’s costs in expended US munitions and damages
A US government watchdog released its first report on Monday on the impact of the Iran war, acknowledging the military’s advanced weapons shortfalls and offering the first public look at the damage to American aircraft, bases and diplomatic outposts in the Middle East.
Much of the information about Operation Epic Fury has been previously reported over the past six months, but the Pentagon inspector general’s report offered the fullest official accounting so far of the conflict’s costs in American lives, taxpayer dollars and physical damage. It included information from the watchdogs for the Defence and State departments as well as the US Agency for International Development.
The report, whose publication was first reported by NBC News, noted that the US war with Iran “has resulted in strategic inventory shortfalls and revealed industrial base bottlenecks for munitions resupply” in regard to advanced weapons.

articles.title: U.S. Navy orders Blackbeard hypersonic missiles in $200M deal
articles.body:
- Castelion announced Sept. 14, 2026, a U.S. Navy production order worth up to $200 million for its Blackbeard hypersonic strike weapon.
- The order follows a June 2026 contract for 50 Blackbeard prototype rounds and moves the air-launched weapon toward fleet production.
The U.S. Navy has ordered production rounds of Castelion’s Blackbeard hypersonic strike weapon in a deal worth up to $200 million, the company announced Sept. 14, 2026. The delivery order covers an initial production lot of the missile and follows a separate June order for 50 early prototype rounds.
The new contract came from Portfolio Acquisition Executive Aviation, through its Future Capability Development and Integration Aviation Rapid Capabilities Cell, and moves Blackbeard out of prototype status and into an initial production run for the fleet.
Blackbeard is an air-launched hypersonic weapon built to strike targets on land or at sea from long range. The Navy plans to carry it on carrier-based aircraft, giving naval air wings a fast, high-speed strike option that adds more weapons to a carrier’s overall magazine without adding more launch platforms.
The order builds on a June 16, 2026, contract in which the Navy paid Castelion $23.4 million for 50 Blackbeard prototypes, known as Early Operational Capability rounds, along with 50 storage and shipping containers. That earlier deal was issued under a Small Business Innovation Research Phase III agreement and was billed at the time as the Navy’s first delivery order for the weapon. Castelion has said that work is due to wrap up in 2027.
“The Navy’s decision to move into production reflects its confidence in the Blackbeard program, and the progress we’ve made together,” said Bryon Hargis, co-founder and CEO of Castelion. “That’s how you get capability to the fleet fast, clear red tape, and partner with industry. We are grateful to PAE(A) for the trust and the urgency. Blackbeard was engineered from day one for the production line and we look forward to delivering this capability to the fleet.”
Castelion has not disclosed how many production rounds the new $200 million ceiling will buy, and the company’s announcement did not include a delivery date for the production lot.
The Blackbeard program has moved quickly since Castelion won its first Navy contracts. In October 2025, the company secured awards to integrate the weapon onto multiple aircraft platforms. Those contracts included work to adapt Blackbeard for carriage on the F/A-18 Super Hornet, covering hardware and software integration, flight testing, and the safety and airworthiness certification the Navy requires before clearing a weapon for storage and use aboard an aircraft carrier.
Castelion has said it has put hundreds of millions of dollars of private investment into Blackbeard, developed in partnership with the Navy, the U.S. Army and the U.S. Air Force. The company has built its production approach around vertical integration and commercial manufacturing techniques, aiming to control cost, quality and schedule across the supply chain rather than relying heavily on outside subcontractors.
Much of that production capacity centers on Project Ranger, a 1,000-acre manufacturing campus the company has built in Rio Rancho, New Mexico, at a cost Castelion has put at more than $250 million. Work under the new delivery order will be split between Project Ranger and Castelion’s original facility in Torrance, California, where the company is headquartered.
Castelion describes Blackbeard as the first U.S. hypersonic weapon designed from the start for industrial-scale production, commercial-level unit costs and continuous flight testing, a break from hypersonic programs that have historically relied on smaller-batch, higher-cost manufacturing. The company has not released a unit cost for the weapon or specified how many rounds it expects to deliver under the new order.
